LIBERAL PARTY ELECTION ADVERTISEMENTS-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, with the latest increase of 9 cents per gallon in petroleum products, gasoline and heating oil prices have increased by as much as 60 cents a gallon in the last year and a half. Yet during the last election campaign the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen), in newspaper advertisements, said "Vote Liberal and the price will stay down". Therefore I move the following motion, under the provisions of Standing Order 43, seconded by the hon. member for Crowfoot (Mr. Malone):
That this House condemn the Liberal government for the deceitful and dastardly way that it has disregarded its campaign promises to keep oil price increases below 18 cents a gallon.

speechtext:

In view of the government's absolute deception of Canadians in taxing energy supplies to pay for its own financial incompetence, thereby imposing unnecessary excise taxes, high interest rates, and spiralling inflation upon all Canadians; and given the government's total failure to produce a long-range industrial development plan so that Canada might realize its true potential heritage for generations to come, I move, seconded by the hon. member for St. Catharines (Mr. Reid):
That the Prime Minister admit to the lying, deceitful practices of his government since its election last February 18, by calling an immediate federal election so that the Canadian people might pass judgment on the dishonest political trickery of the Liberal Party of Canada.

INCREASE IN PRICES-AID FOR PEOPLE IN REMOTE AREAS- MOTION UNDER S O. 43
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the motion that I shall move under the provisions of Standing Order 43 is with regard to recent increases in petroleum products. Considering the serious impact such increases in energy costs have as they are passed through to northern residents of our country, to whom energy and transportation costs represent the single most contributing factor in already disproportionately high living costs, I move:
That this House request the government to produce forthwith and lay before the House measures designed to shelter those Canadians who live in isolated, remote and northern regions of our country, from the effects of the latest unjustified increases in energy costs, and to consider the special circumstances of residents in such areas as they relate to the already excessive costs of transportation and being able to maintain an adequate and equitable standard of living.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity. Earlier this week a riot broke out in the Matsqui institution at Abbotsford, British Columbia, during which over 50 per cent of the medium security complex was destroyed by fire. Reports indicate that 200 members of the RCMP, 20 Matsqui police officers, and over 150 troops from Canadian Forces Base, Chilliwack, were called into action to restore order.
Because of the challenge to authority and the wanton destruction of facilities built by taxpayers' money, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Surrey-White Rock-North Delta (Mr. Friesen), the following motion under the provisions of Standing Order 43:
That the Solicitor General assure the public that those responsible for this act of destruction will be held accountable, and suitable penalties be imposed, including the withholding of pay, the use of the prison population in the rebuilding of the facilities, and any other procedures available to lessen the financial burden on the Canadian taxpayers.

The Canadian shipping industry was shocked to learn that the government is again considering a further increase in Seaway tolls, tolls that have increased by over 100 per cent since 1978, and on an industry now subject to world prices for bunker fuel oil while other modes of transport engaged in international trade enjoy the benefit of a heavily subsidized domestic oil price. speechtext: On a point of order, Madam Speaker. I would like to gain some knowledge of the Standing Orders of the House. speechtext:
Order, please. If I ask hon. members not to comment on my rulings, it is obvious that I cannot do so myself. Besides, the minister is in a very difficult situation because he cannot comment on that point of order without referring to the question on which I have ruled already. On several occasions the minister gave explanations to the House concerning his conduct. His explanations were accepted by the House until
further notice. Should another opportunity arise, I am confident that when other questions are put to the minister he will give to the House whatever explanations he may want to give, but he may not do so at this time.

speakeroldname: Hon. Yvon Pinard (President of the Privy Council):
speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, often in the past when the Chair ruled against a question of privilege based on the criteria established in practice and in the Standing Orders, a member could still rise on a point of order. So it is in this manner that I rise now on a point of order, which is not the question of privilege raised by the Minister of Justice (Mr. Chretien) which you rejected, because points of order can be raised by any member of this House. Now it is strictly forbidden, according to the rules, to make allegations about a member, and it is clear that during question period the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark) accused the Minister of Justice and made allegations by saying that he was not doing his job and was not taking his responsibilities seriously. That is clearly against the rules of this House. I am not raising a question of privilege, as you have already given your ruling on that, but I am rising, as an ordinary member, on a point of order to ask the Leader of the Opposition to withdraw his very serious allegations about the Minister of Justice, if he has the courage to do so.
Madam Speaker, we are dealing with procedure, and it is indeed true that you have ruled against the question of privilege, perhaps before completely hearing out the Minister of Justice, but that was your ruling and I do not wish to go back on it. I will abide by your ruling and not comment on it. However, by rising on a point of order, I submit that it is the Chair's duty to ensure that no member of this House, whatever his title, be allowed to make allegations about anyone. In this case, the Leader of the Opposition is clearly at fault for having, during the Question Period, taken the opportunity to clearly, directly and unequivocally suggest that the Minister of Justice was not doing his job. I think that we cannot let that go by unchallenged and that is why I am rising on a point of order because 1 would like you to ask the Leader of the Opposition to have the courage to stand in his place and withdraw his accusations.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, if there is any duty at all on a member, his first duty is not to attempt to do indirectly what would be wrong to do directly, and that is to question a ruling of the Chair. I must say I am rather surprised at my hon. friend moving in the direction he did, having regard to the skill and understanding he has of the rules.
The second thing is, it is incumbent upon every member of the House to address the House and the issues in a parliamentary way. If you examine the blues of the exchanges that took place you will find that the language used by the Right Hon. Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark) in the House was
June 4, 1981

absolutely parliamentary. It was not out of order; in fact, it was in order. This place is not any thing else but a place of debate where strong positions are taken on issues that are important. Of course, that must be done within the confines of appropriate parliamentary language. I do not believe that any unparliamentary language was used, and I am sure if it was the Leader of the Opposition would be the first to recognize it.

On this particular point, Madam Speaker, the question is always a very difficult and narrow one. I think I have been able to detect during the exercise by the government House leader and others on the government side this question of attributing motives to members of the opposition, trying to silence them in that way. What I would suggest to the House leader is the difference is this, that if the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark) said the Minister of Juctice (Mr. Chretien) would be failing in his duty if he failed to do something with a report, that would not be attributing a motive at all; that is, if he failed to do something having received a report. On the other hand, if I were to suggest that the intervention by the government House leader was an attempt to intimidate the Chair, then that would be a clear attribution of a motive to the government House leader.
I have used that example merely to establish the distinction in his mind, and I trust in the minds of my colleagues in the House. Unfortunately every time there seems to be criticism of the government side there is immediately this attempt to rise and say that members of the opposition are attributing motives. That is not the case. I would hold that there was no such thing on the part of the Right Hon. Leader of the Opposition at all, in any way. This is merely a misinterpretation of the rules by the government House leader to his advantage.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the point of order originated with the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Pinard) and it was followed by a comment by the hon. member for Nepean-Carleton (Mr. Baker). I do not want to talk about the substance of the matter because I know you have ruled on the substance. But there is a clear difference in this House with regard to the rules relating to unparliamentary language, which is listed in Beauchesne-though not all unparliamentary words are listed there-and the imputation of motives. Citation 322 of Beauchesne clearly states:
It has been formally ruled by Speakers that a statement by a member respecting himself and particularly within his own knowledge must be accepted, but it is not unparliamentary temperately to criticize statements made by a member as being contrary to the facts; but no imputation of intentional falsehood is permissible.
That is the key, and it is very easy to use very parliamentary language in the imputation of motives. But that is not what is at issue.
1 submit there is another reference to which Your Honour should turn, and that is 316(e) of Beauschesne, fifth edition, which clearly states:
Besides the prohibitions contained in S.O. 35, it has been sanctioned by usage that a member, while speaking, must not:
(e) impute bad motives or motives different from those acknowledged to a
member;-
I submit what was done this afternoon clearly contravened the practices of this House and in no way dealt with unparliamentary language.

Madam Speaker, I am sure Your Honour will find that there is no point of order, as there was no question of privilege, but it might be useful, since several highly exercised ministers of the Crown have been engaged in this matter in their usual intemperate way, for me to review the record of what happened here today.
I should say that it is of more than passing interest to note the unease in the government benches having to do with the uranium cartel and whether the facts about that cartel will be made public or held secret. That is the matter which is of the deepest political interest and, I think, of interest to the country.
Let us review what happened. What happened was that the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Ouellet) said solemnly to this House of Commons that he would make public the findings of the inquiry into the uranium cartel. That is what he said; he put it on the record. He has today reinterpreted his statement to say that public means private.

speechtext: Order, please. The Right Hon. Leader of the Opposition is debating the question. That was the whole substance of what was discussed during the question period. speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
It seems to me that two things have been discussed. The Minister of Justice gave explanations about the procedure he was following respecting a certain report, and I ruled that there was no question of privilege.
Then a further point of order having to do with imputing motives was raised. At the time of the deliberations I did not have the feeling that motives had been imputed, but I do recognize that there is quite a lot of noise in the House and I sometimes do not hear all of what is said in the House. My impression was that the Leader of the Opposition was criticizing the actions of the minister and expressing an opinion about those actions of the minister, but that he had not imputed bad motives.
I can do two things with respect to this particular question. Conversation is rather rapid in the House. I was going to ask the Right Hon. Leader of the Opposition if he thought he had imputed motives and, if he did, he might want to withdraw; but he has just now told the House that he has not imputed motives, and I am not in a position to contradict him at this point.
I will look at the records. If I find that motives have not been imputed-because my impression now is that motives have not been imputed-I will not come back to the House with this question. If I feel that motives have been imputed, I will then take the necessary actions to see that things are conducted in this House in a parliamentary way.

Have there been any changes in assigned responsibilities for the surveillance of coastal waters since March 4, 1976 and, if so, what are they?

speakeroldname: Mr. D. M. Collenette (Parliamentary Secretary to President of the Privy Council):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
In so far as the Department of the Environment is concerned: No.
In so far as the Department of Fisheries and Oceans is concerned: up to December 31, 1976, waters outside 12 miles on Canada's east coast were managed through the International Commission of the Northwest Atlantic Fisheries (ICNAF). Under the auspices of this commission, a joint scheme of international enforcement was established which enabled member countries to conduct surveillance and inspections of fishing vessels of all member nations which fished in the ICNAF area. Canada played a lead role in this scheme and in addition to ships of the Department of Fisheries and Oceans utilized ships and aircraft of Department of National Defence and Department of Transport. Waters inside 12 miles which
were not included in the ICNAF scheme were also patrolled but were under Canadian management.
On the west coast, there was limited foreign fishing activity outside 12 miles. The major countries were the U.S., Poland, Japan and the U.S.S.R. Management of the major U.S. and Canadian fisheries (halibut and salmon) were by international agreement through the International Pacific Halibut Commission (IPHC) and the International Pacific Salmon Fisheries Commission (IPSFC). Bilateral agreements with Poland and the U.S.S.R. were in effect to avoid gear conflicts with Canadian salmon vessels fishing outside 12 miles. Waters inside 12 miles were patrolled by DFO ships. Surveillance outside 12 miles was conducted by both DFO and DND vessels.

As of January 1, 1977, with the declaration of the 200-mile limit, Canada took over management of fish stocks inside 200 nautical miles of baselines along her coasts. Foreign nations were permitted to continue to fish under licence in this new zone for stocks surplus to the needs of Canadian fishermen. Their fishing operations were then subject to Canadian regulations, licences and enforcement programs. Surveillance operations within the new zone were also brought under Canadian management and violations were handled in Canadian courts. Surveillance is conducted by DFO ships with assistance from the Department of National Defence as required and through interdepartmental arrangements. In addition, Canadian observers are frequently on board foreign fishing vessels.
In waters of the former ICNAF area which are not inside 200 miles the ICNAF scheme of joint enforcement is continuing under the North Atlantic Fisheries Organization (NAFO) which is a successor to ICNAF. Waters under NAFO management are mainly the Flemish Cap and the southern and eastern extremeties of the Grand Banks. On the west coast, agreements between Canada and the U.S. are ongoing to provide co-operative management and enforcement of the halibut and salmon fisheries; however, neither country conducts any fishing activities for these species in waters of the other country.
In so far as the Department of National Defence is concerned: there has been no change in assigned responsibilities for the surveillance of coastal waters. However, the degree of support provided by the Canadian Forces to assist other government departments in carrying out their regulatory responsibilities, does change in accordance with circumstances.
In so far as the Department of Transport is concerned: yes.

This merely confirms my view that during the first three days, the debate was on the bill generally.

Now, this particular item is very narrow and deals with a definition of "manufacturer or producer". One of the major changes in this bill has been to introduce the concept of a marginal manufacturer and to bootleg into the Canadian tax structure a value added tax in the guise of an excise tax.

At page 2, paragraph (3), we find under subparagraph (e) an amended definition of manufacturer or producer:
(e) any person who sells gasoline, diesel fuel or aviation fuel, other than a
person who sells such goods exclusively and directly to consumers,
In this case, a person having bought wholesale quantities of fuel, diesel or gasoline puts them in small barrels to sell them to dealers. I think that my colleague, the hon. member for Burlington (Mr. Kempling) will explain the situation of a petroleum products dealer in his riding who happens to be affected by this section of the bill.

Now, why are we getting this value added tax? We are starting out with this particular point because there is no way that one can accept in the definitions clause these various definitions of manufacturers or producers. If the minister is having difficulty locating it I will read from the original act as to who is a manufacturer or producer. I can read a half page of very close text but it simply says the assignee, the trustee of a legitimate manufacturer or producer, the user of a patent or other right to goods, departments of government and other public authorities, and sellers of cosmetics.
June 4, 1981

The first amendment in the bill deals with sellers of cosmetics. Strangely enough, the very first definition in Bill C-57 is that of "cosmetics". We are dealing now with the definition clause. A general debate was called for because of the limited debate beforehand. Now we are getting down to the nitty-gritty, the start. We are just lifting the corner of the box on the idea of marginal manufacturers.
The hon. member for Capilano (Mr. Huntington) and many others will show what the Minister of Finance (Mr. Mac-Eachen) is trying to do by establishing this category of person and what the effect of the tax will be. We can show the bottom line to the public because they are the ones who will pay it. Not only is it a value added tax in the case of some marginal manufacturers, but in the case of distributors of cosmetics there is a transfer of the manufacturers' excise tax to the wholesale level. This is a deviation from the principle of an excise tax at the manufacturers level. This is what we are supposed to have.
We will fight the indexing of the excise tax based upon the cost of living. Naturally this will save or eliminate the necessity of the Minister of Finance having to come to Parliament to obtain an increase in taxes or an increase in his revenues, simply by letting the percentage tax or the ad valorem tax accumulate and snowball.
The other night the minister responsible for financial institutions received the permission of the House to put in a different ways and means motion which changed the base period. It did not reduce the tax, but in essence it will raise perhaps as much as $25 million more by reason of the changes.
It is incumbent upon the House to realize fully what it is doing. I am satisfied that hon. members on the government side did not sit on the committee as parts of a floating goon squad, brought in from time to time to make a quorum. They sat there understanding and following the briefs, presentations and representations made by the public. They will realize that a fundamental change is being effected on the excise tax.
Part IV is a direct tax on revenue. In fact, part of it has already been declared illegal by the Alberta Court of Appeal. We will have more to say about that later on. In this particular amendment we are seeing a small corner of the box being lifted on the idea of marginal manufacturers and the application of the tax on those individuals. Since they have purchased goods on which they will not pay or be charged with excise tax, they will have to charge and obtain from their customers an excise tax based upon the increase in value because of the packaging or servicing of the commodity. This will be a value added tax.
I do not have any intention of going on at great length, but I hope some of my colleagues will deal with this particular point. We will come back to it as we deal with other amendments. We had an amendment to include diesel fuel in the bill. That has been left without amendment, but it is very instructive to see the amendment which follows that which we are trying to
Excise Tax
delete. According to clause 1(3), a manufacturer or producer shall be:
-any person who, by himself or through another person acting for him, assembles, blends, mixes, cuts to size, dilutes, bottles, packages, repackages or otherwise prepares goods for sale, other than a person who so prepares goods in a retail store for sale in that store exclusively and directly to consumers.
What about the Liquor Control Board of the province of Ontario which buys rum, sherry and other spirits in bulk quantities and bottles them? Are they to be marginal manufacturers? Since they are part of the government of Ontario, presumably they will fall under the rule established by the Alberta Court of Appeal, that one level of government cannot tax the activities of another level of government, in the case of gas owned, produced and distributed by the government of the province of Alberta or an agency thereof.
Also it would be very interesting to see whether the Government of Canada would dare to impose any tax on the Liquor Control Board of the province of Quebec, or La Regie des Alcools du Quebec, on its wine importing and bottle operations. One could speculate at length on the activities.
We will see just how far this will go. Will it apply to an importer of coffee or an importer of tea who imports in bulk and packages under a private label for one of the big chain stores or department stores? I am not too sure whether that kind of service will be included. They are goods which the importer has blended, mixed and packaged. Presumably those goods will be subject to another tax by the Government of Canada. Whether there is a limited value or a notch is not disclosed; at least, I have not been able to find it. But no doubt there will be excise tax bulletins-explanatory-which will have the force of law. Hon. members opposite will have no more participation in etablishing those details than I will, but we will suddenly find them in force like statutes. All too often we will find public servants, when one protests or begins to examine these provisions, saying, "Well, they were made by Parliament." That is nonsense. These interpretation bulletins, explanatory texts or excise tax bulletins are internal regulations made by the department itself. They have the force of law.
I am objecting to the concept of the marginal manufacturer being brought in under this act, not necessarily at his manufacturers level, but as I pointed out earlier, in so far as a distributor of cosmetics is concerned, at the wholesale level. I am opposed to this particular amendment to the act and would urge the House to support my friend from Etobicoke Centre (Mr. Wilson) and myself in having this portion of the amending bill deleted.

speakeroldname: Hon. Marcel Lambert (Edmonton West) (for Mr. Blenkarn) moved:
subtopic: EXCISE TAX ACT AND EXCISE ACT
speechtext:
Motion No. 4.
That Bill C-57, an act to amend the Excise Tax Act and the Excise Act and to provide for a revenue tax in respect of petroleum and gas, be amended in Clause 1 by striking out lines 1 to 23 at page 4.
He said: Mr. Speaker, this is what I would call the second highest summit in this particular bill, one which I think from the point of view of government represents the worst departure that we as members of Parliament could possibly contemplate in that the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen), in proposing paragraph 6 on page 4 of Bill C-57, is asking Parliament to give him a blank cheque in perpetuity. He is asking that the excise tax on an alcoholic and tobacco subgroup be indexed on the basis of what was asked in the bill on a quarterly basis, which means that every quarter the government would examine the CPI and adjust the ad valorem tax of 9 per cent by the
amount of the quarterly CPI advance-and up would go the tax by that calculation. If the tax is 9 per cent and the CPI is x, you get 9 plus x. At the sixth month rest we would have the 9 per cent plus y, which is the difference between the third month and the sixth month, and there would be a calculation. The calculation would be 9 plus x times 9 plus y divided by four, so that the introduction of the quarterly CPI operated as a snowball.
Much as any one of us likes to receive compound interest on our savings accounts or on our government bonds, the government was receiving tax on a compound basis. There was great objection to this. The first people to object were the chairmen of the liquor boards of Canada. There were delegates from the provinces of New Brunswick, Quebec, Ontario and one other province, if my memory serves me correctly, who indicated just what this measure would mean to the liquor boards across the country which, every three months, would have to recalculate the federal excise tax, as well as other changes with regard to the sale of wine, beer and spirits. The additional cost would amount to hundreds of thousands of dollars per year and would make their business very difficult. Such is the puritan ethic in this country that the government has the freedom to do anything it likes as long as it goes after alcohol. In other words, the end justifies the means. Of course, precisely the same steps were taken with regard to old demon tobacco.
It is not only the calculation of the tax based upon the CPI in the subgroup which is affected; that in turn is affected by the general CPI, by variations in the Canadian dollar, by conditions abroad where wines and spirits may be purchased, and by all sorts of influences that are beyond the control of distillers, brewers, vintners and the liquor commissions. I have some things to say about the practices of the liquor commissions too, Mr. Speaker, as I think they are highly objectionable.
If the House accepts the principle of this tax, then 1 can guarantee that, as sure as the sun rises in the eastern heavens tomorrow, the Minister of Finance will index tax in some other sector because it is so convenient. It is made to order for the bureaucracy and it is made to order for a minister of finance such as the one we have at the present time who does not like to face the House or to discuss the parlous state of the country's finances openly with members of the House.
We could find that the system will be applied to building materials or to educational materials. In the bill, schedule V deals with construction material and schedule IV deals with petroleum products. There is a culprit for that one, the provincial treasurer of Ontario, who in his last budget fixed the provincial tax on an ad valorem basis and a quarterly index.
If the price of gasoline goes up quickly in Ontario we know that we can thank the gentlemen who have devised this system so that they can shrug it off, as the Minister of Finance proposes to do. They can say that Parliament voted this formula and that it is beyond their control. This Parliament should be ashamed of itself for even considering it. Members
June 4, 1981

of the government should be ashamed of themselves if they support the minister in this.
The protests were loud and long when it was proposed to index the tax quarterly. Then the minister indicated, just the other night, that he would need a ways and means motion in order to change it because on the basis of representations made by the industry-I wonder which brewers and which distillers got to the government-it was decided that the indexing would be annual. Since an annual indexing would mean a reduction of the tax, I insisted that there was no need for a ways and means motion. The minister, however, insisted that there would be more revenue. When I was shown the proposal, I immediately saw the shell under which the bean lies! The base period has been changed in the amendment.
I should like to read to the House what has been said about this move by the Brewers Association of Canada which put a fair assessment on the effect of the amendment proposed by the minister the other night. The minister was modest-immeasurably so-when he said that this would yield about the same revenues. A letter of yesterday's date from the Brewers Association of Canada reads:
The annual increase in excise levies on beer will increase a further $1.6 million, an increase of 10 per cent from the $16.5 million originally proposed by the indexing provisions contained in the October, 1980, budget. The increase in excise levies on distilled spirits will be approximately $6.0 million, an increase of 17 per cent over the original increase of $36 million,-
We see that as a result of this little deal in the excise tax on beer and spirits distilled in Canada the government is going to get some $60 million. That is the value of the tax and we have not even gone into the wine area yet. The letter continues:
These increases arise not because of the change from quarterly to annual indexing, which would have resulted in a decrease in revenue, not an increase, but because of a change in the timing of the changes and the base for calculating the increases.
Tables are attached to show this. The letter goes on:
Had the point of indexing on an annual basis been set at October 1, rather than September 1 (still using the relationship of the Alcoholic Beverage Consumer Price Index for the year ended June 30, 1981, compared with that of June 30, 1980, for adjusting the excise rates), the inequity caused by the method chosen as outlined in the most recent amendment would not have been as great. From Exhibit C attached, it may be seen that the revenue from beer would be virtually the same as it would have been under the original Bill C-57. For spirits, the increase in revenue would still be higher, but probably only half as much as a September 1 date for annual indexing would cause.
Since the minister listened to industry once, perhaps he would listen a second time. It asks that the amendment put forward by the minister be amended to change the date of annual indexing from September 1 to October 1. This would diminish the tax. We must look after the Canadian public after all. Some Canadian beer and spirits are sold abroad but, strangely enough, the excise tax is not charged on spirits sold abroad. It is Canadians, and Canadians only, who have to pay the shot.
The minister will come back echoing the words of his colleagues in cabinet who say that the government needs the money. That is piffle. It is the minister's proposed spending
Excise Tax
programs which come out as "we need the money." The cart is before the horse, somewhat like an individual who might say "I am going to buy a $13,000 car. Now I have to earn a salary, and earn that much in order to pay for it." That is about the same logic. The average individual conducts his affairs on the basis of, say, a salary of $15,000 a year, that it costs him so much to live, and he can do this and that with it. In other words, you tailor your suit according to the cloth you have.
The government does not do that. The government and its bureaucrats lay out spending programs. Right now we are listening to the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin) and other ministers proposing to spend money like it never was in style. Then the government turns around and says, "We need the money." What do you think it is going to do? The government is going out to raid and plunder the resources of the western provinces, as it is doing. It is doing this because it is strapped for money. The Liberals are the ones who brought in this petroleum products equalization program encouraging people to consume offshore petroleum at prices up to $43. In order to compensate for that, the government tells the people of Alberta that they will get $17.75 per barrel of oil. Oil is a disappearing, non-renewable resource. If there ever was an idiot's program, this is it. I will define it for you. It is the bread and circuses of emperor Trudeau for the mobs in central Canada, as was done in old Roman times. The Liberals' popularity is bought on the backs of the resources of the western provinces. The government would not dare do it on the resources of the central provinces. This philosophy leads the government to that end.
The government needed $3.5 billion this year to pay for subsidized offshore crude. Where does the government get that money? The government takes it from the hides of all Canadians because so much a gallon is being tacked on. But the government did not do that; it is part of the blended Canadian price. Then the government takes some more. Hon. members should look at how much the federal share has gone up. In this bill we see an 8 per cent tax on revenue from petroleum and natural gas. This is an illegal tax on natural gas owned by the province, says the appeal court of the province of Alberta. But this bill says nothing about that. It just asks us to go ahead and legislate in the face of that opinion.
There is no need for this insatiable appetite for money by the government, that every dollar earned must be taxed, that every service performed must be taxed. I have had national revenue officials write articles and tell me personally that every day I earn my salary there is a portion caught by the Income Tax Act, and at that moment I owe it to the Crown. In the government's mind, that is the subservience of the individual to the state. How totally wrong that is. It is the state which is the servant of the people. The individuals, whether corporate or personal, are not the servants of the state. Nor do they exist for the glorification of the state. Nor should they accept greater direction. We now see a strong central government. They say-

June 4, 1981
Excise Tax

-a planned economy worthy of Caesar, that is all it is. It is a type of state control with which socialists are rather more familiar, but they are interventionists and economic planners.

Those words sound so much better in French than they do in English!
That is why I ask my colleagues to help me oppose this pernicious tax. It is the principle of levying an indexed tax.
The government is interested in inflation. I see some members opposite shrugging their shoulders as though they do not know what is contained in the bill. So what, they say. Of course this government is interested in inflation. It would be far better for the government if inflation were at 100 per cent because government revenues would rise. The government could spend more and more money.

speechtext:
Pretty soon, as in the Weimar Republic, people would be taking home their week's pay in a wheelbarrow, losing 10 per cent on the way.
I find this reproachable, which is a mild term. I am disappointed. It is an abdication of the government's absolute duty to fight inflation. But what does the government do? It kneels down with inflation and says "Let's go along together, sweetheart." Why do I say this? Because the more inflation there is, the higher the revenues to the government. This government's philosophy is a total abdication of the government's responsibility.
This trend started in 1969. At that time the government began indexing old age pensions on a modest basis. Then the old sheer started cutting into the salami sausage. The increase was to be 2 per cent if the cost of living increase exceeded 4 per cent. The 2 per cent was the maximum. Public service pensions were fixed that way at that time as well. Then the figure of 7 per cent came in. It would be the amount of the annual increase for the OAS, GIS, war veterans, what have you. Cushions under everybody, public servant superannuates as well as the superannuates of the armed services, except they had limitations on age.
We have now reached the point where the OAS and GIS are indexed quarterly and war veterans disability pensions, POW compensation and other pensions from the government are indexed annually on the total amount of the CPI increase of the year before. Cushions. Yet we hear fatuous statements from the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) such as that they have wrestled inflation to the ground. He would not know inflation if it stared him in the face!
This is their answer. This is the ultimate. This measure should never pass. If the federal government does it, the provinces will do it. Some of the provinces are already emulating the federal government. It does not make a bit of difference; that does not make it right. John Q. Public is not only
getting stomped on the neck but is getting his backside kicked doubly by this proposal.
As far as I am concerned, this shall not pass. Why do we get it at this time? Is this a ploy? Already we have seen some bargaining from quarterly indexing to annual indexing, which would have been a reduction. However, as I say, the bee moved under the shelves and they changed the base period, with the net result that the Canadian public will pay more in taxes. Why? So that the government can design more and bigger spending programs in the future.
I was looking over some schedules supplied to me in great detail by the Brewers Association. Presumably there will be some from the distillers as well as from the wine industry. The Ontario government is doing something to help develop the wine industry in its province. Strangely enough, we look upon our wine industry as part of a booze industry, as though there is something wrong with it. European countries, and in fact any country worth its salt, considers it a part of agriculture. I am sure some members opposite from the Niagara peninsula will say that their grape growers are as much a part of the agricultural industry as the orchard-the apple growers, peach growers, cherry growers and vegetable growers.
Ontario is trying to develop a credible wine industry, as is British Columbia. More power to them. There is nothing wrong with wine, taken in moderation. However, when a province takes artificial steps, as Ontario has done, by imposing a tariff on non-Ontario wines, I find that reprehensible. It is an open breach of the spirit of confederation. Having listened to the stuff that came from Queen's Park during the constitutional debate about the spirit of confederation, to my mind their remarks are pretty shallow. Our bucolic Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) should do some of the showboating he has done in other areas in the area of agriculture.
I next want to deal with the change in the tax on wines. I quote from the bill:
24. (1) There shall be imposed, levied and collected the following excise taxes:
(a)	a tax of sixty cents per gallon on wines of all kinds containing not more than seven per cent of absolute alcohol by volume; and
(b)	a tax of one dollar and twenty-five cents per gallon on wines of all kinds containing more than seven per cent of absolute alcohol by volume.
Further:
24. (1) There shall be imposed, levied and collected the following excise taxes:
(a)	a tax of thirteen and two-tenth cents per litre on wines of all kinds containing not more than seven per cent of absolute ethyl alcohol by volume; and
(b)	a tax of twenty-seven and five-tenth cents per litre on wines of all kinds containing more than seven per cent of absolute ethyl alcohol by volume.
In the original act, we see there is a tax of 25 cents per gallon on wines of all kinds containing not more than 7 per cent of absolute alcohol by volume and a tax of 50 cents per gallon on wines of other kinds. This tax, goes up to $1.25. There is an increase of 150 per cent in the tax on wine stronger than 7 per cent. I am just wondering whether the hon. member for Lincoln (Mr. Mackasey) will take part in the debate here regarding the brandy manufacturers and what is going to be done with all the domestic brandy manufactured from the
June 4, 1981

surplus grapes the government of Ontario bought in order to save the industry from an absolute glut two or three years ago.
Those are the things you see when you start examining this terrible bill. The people of Canada are being taken to the tax cleaners. We have only started; wait until we get it all. Even with educational tools and equipment this tax applies. You should read the words used, Mr. Speaker, because what you have been accustomed to considering as educational equipment need not now be so considered and therefore be subject to tax. All this turns on is the word "designed". These are the things one finds so objectionable in this particular bill.
Having said all these things on this question of the indexing of the excise tax, I plead with my colleagues in this House, particularly those on the government side, to pause and recognize the nefarious results of the acceptance of the principle contained at the top of page 4, subsection (6) of clause 1 of this bill. I certainly hope all hon. members of this House would unite and accept the amendment I have put forward on behalf of my colleague, the hon. member for Mississauga South (Mr. Blenkarn).

speakeroldname: Mr. Bob Rae (Broadview-Greenwood) (for Mr. Riis) moved:
subtopic: EXCISE TAX ACT AND EXCISE ACT
speechtext:
Motion No. 5.
That Bill C-57, an act to amend the Excise Tax Act and to provide for a revenue tax in respect of petroleum and gas, be amended in clause 1 by striking out lines 1 to 23 at page 4.
He said: Mr. Speaker, it is always difficult to follow the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) because he certainly covers the waterfront on these particular issues. What I want to do with regard to this amendment is to come back to some fundamental principles in relation to the taxes we are discussing in this bill.
It is important to remember that the taxes we are discussing today are excise or sales taxes, and federal excise tax has been a matter of some controversy when one reflects on events over the past couple of years. Excise taxes are by their very nature controversial because they are extremely visible and can also be extremely regressive.
I want to deal in particular with the tax on beer and the effect indexing that tax will have on the average Canadian consumer. We always approach this subject with some ambivalence, because part of the Canadian ethic, as has been described by many people, and most recently today by the hon. member for Edmonton West, is that our attitude to alcohol in our culture is an extremely ambivalent one. Overconsumption of alcohol causes tremendous problems for individuals who suffer from that problem, and it causes tremendous difficulties for the families, the people close and dear to the people who suffer from overconsumption of alcohol.
Still, the consumption of alcohol in our society now is not generally regarded as evil. It is something that is regarded as a form of pleasure; it is, I think in a society which has, thank goodness, become less puritanical than that of our predecessors, something we can engage in without shame.
I want to express my support for what the hon. member for Edmonton West said about the wine industry. It is extraordinary that in Canada we do not regard the wine industry as part and parcel of our agricultural industry, something that should be given far more encouragement by the government than is the case.
The consumer of beer, I think, would be shocked to hear that 45 per cent of the retail price of a bottle of beer goes to his federal and provincial governments in the form of taxes. This puts us very, very high in the international sweepstakes on beer taxation. Spain is the lowest with 6 per cent, West Germany has 20 per cent, the United States comes in at the same, 20 per cent, the United Kingdom comes in at 35 per cent, Canada is on the high side with 45 per cent, with the highest being Ireland at 53 per cent. One can see by comparison with a number of other countries that Canada already taxes its beer industry at a very high rate.

June 4, 1981
Excise Tax
1 am focusing on the beer industry because it is an industry that is particularly hard hit by this measure. I am not excluding the effect it has on the hard spirit or wine industries. Other members of my party will be focusing on the effect on the wine industry as this bill progresses, but I want to focus on the beer industry.
It is important to note a report submitted to the Department of Finance by a commodity tax review group in 1976. Quoting from this report, it states:
Beer is consumed by approximately 12 million persons in Canada each year who are predominantly in the lower and middle socioeconomic groups. Because excise taxes are regressive, it is these persons (particularly in lower income groups) who pay the greatest proportion of the taxes on beer. These are also the families who would benefit most favourably, financially, from a reduction in taxes on beer-in some instances more than from an elimination of the personal income tax.
It is that regressivity that I think we should put at the forefront of the question. If it can be shown, and I think it can, that excise taxes have a regressive effect as a form of taxation, and if it can be shown that these taxes fall more heavily on the working people and people who are earning less than $15,000 a year, then we have to ask ourselves why does the government decide that this particular form of excise tax on alcohol, beer, wine and spirits is going to be subject to indexation, an automatic increase regardless of the impact it has on the industry, regardless of the impact it has on consumption patterns, and regardless of the relative burden of taxation as between beer, wines and spirits?
There are really, I guess, two separate questions here which I would like to touch on. The first is the question of principle which was discussed at some length by the hon. member for Edmonton West, and that is the principle whether we should be indexing any of the excise taxes on alcohol at all, and whether the principle of indexation is one which we should endorse. The second is the impact of indexation on this particular industry. Does it really make sense at this particular time? It is with those two questions that I want to deal before the dinner hour.
The first question is the principle of indexation. At a time when the government is talking about the need to create an anti-inflationary psychology in the population and telling us that there is no quick fix but that we have to be determined to hunker down and to fight inflation in a real way, it seems to me ironic, to put it mildly-and I think in fact it is hypocritical, to describe it accurately-for the government then to turn around and say it is going to impose a system or notion of tax on this particular industry which is based on the phenomenon of inflation, which benefits from the phenomenon of inflation and which means that government revenues will automatically grow in response to inflation.
The government can say, and I have heard it said-it has been said in committee-that there is nothing wrong with indexation because we have accepted the principle of indexation, that it was proposed by the Conservative party, and so forth. It was accepted by the Liberal party, although now it is
starting to have some second or third thoughts about it if one listens to the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen). We have accepted the principle of indexation with respect to personal deductions involving personal income tax. But there is a very real difference, because that kind of indexation to increase deductions does two things. First, it guarantees that there is a limit on the revenue which the government can automatically receive from inflation, and at the same time it provides compensation to those Canadians who are suffering from the impact of inflation, the economic theory and the principle being that if Canadians receive some kind of tax relief, the chances are that by providing that kind of cushion all Canadians will not be forced to go to the private market in order to find their own private solutions to the very serious public problem of inflation.
So there really is no point comparing the principle of the indexation of personal deductions, which we accept, and the principle of indexation of the excise tax on alcohol, which has the opposite effect from that intended. The indexation of alcohol has the effect of increasing the price of the product in addition to whatever other increases in the cost of the product there are.
The cost of beer, wine or spirits can go up as a result of a number of factors. In the case of some industries it goes up because of the increase in the import cost due to the devaluation of the dollar or in the case of the beer industry it could be because of an increase in the cost of barley which is set by the Canadian Wheat Board. This is something we do not mind; we want the producers to get their fair price. Or it could increase because of labour costs or whatever other costs there are in the industry. But to add to those costs an automatic benefit to the government in response to inflation simply fuels inflation.
As I say, as far as revenue goes, when one looks at the whole range of the government's sources of revenue-and when we talk about public spending we are dealing with tens of billions of dollars-the revenue windfall to the government is not significant. What is significant, though, is that it is one of inflation's minor victories. It is a minor victory for the federal government in simply deciding it is going to get into the act and it is going to benefit from inflation, but the effect it will have on the consumer will be negative. It will simply increase the cost and will guarantee that costs will continually and perpetually be going up.
The second principle with which I want to deal is the other effect it has and the reason it is wrong. It is wrong because it takes away the discretionary ability of the government year in and year out to deal with the relative burden of taxation on any one of the industries in question. We know that in Canada the relative burden of taxation on the beer industry is high compared with the liquor industry, for a number of historic reasons. In other words, beer is taxed relatively more in relation to hard spirits in Canada than it is in most other countries. The figures are very clear. There are all sorts of factors. There are health factors. There are consumption factors. Employment questions are involved. All these consider-
June 4, 1981

ations should be dealt with on an annual basis by the government.
If the government is going to engage in a serious change- which I suggest to the minister indexation is-and if the government is going to lock in current taxation patterns, then surely to goodness the minister has an obligation to put before the House more information with respect to consumption and with respect to the relative effects on health of the consumption of beer versus the consumption of hard liquor. Surely to goodness the government has an obligation, if this is the kind of permanent regime in the taxation of alcohol that we will have, to conduct socioeconomic and health studies in order to justify this kind of change. The government has not done that. The government has simply introduced this tax for one very simple reason, and that is that it sees the Tory provinces doing it. The government sees that Quebec has done it. Just two weeks ago Frank Miller put in his budget the notion of an ad valorem tax and the notion of an automatic benefit to the province, so the federal government has said that in a world of sinners it will not be the only angel and will get into the act in order to guarantee it will get its share of the revenues as well.
What an illogical system! What an absurd justification for that kind of policy! What kind of impact will this have on the average consumer and on the industry? What study is being done by the federal government on the effect on consumption? What effect will there be on the health of the industry and on the health of the consumers of these products?
Before five o'clock I want to make one final point by saying that if the government is going to be introducing a commodity tax proposal before this House-as the Minister of Finance suggested in committee he would do-why introduce this year a change which has not really been studied, its impact has not been examined and the committee has not had an opportunity to look at all of the implications of moving to this system of indexation and making a significant change in our commodity taxes?
This matter has not really been examined by this House or by the committee. I say to the minister, put this measure off. We will debate it. We can keep on debating it. There is no need to introduce it this year. Let us carry on with the existing system. The government can increase the taxes of whatever industry it decides by two cents, a nickel or a dime. That is the way governments have always conducted their business. It is deplorable, but that is the way it is done. However, the government should not introduce such a major change respecting the taxation of commodities which are important to employment and providers of what I still think are innocent sources of pleasure for the Canadian public.
