speechtext:
that Bill C-246, to amend the Official Secrets Act, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I take pleasure in taking this opportunity to speak on this bill, to amend the Official Secrets Act. I do not think it is any secret that although the bill bears my name it really is merely a carbon copy of a bill introduced many years ago by my predecessor, Mr. Gerald Baldwin, Q.C. I think he is well known as the father of information and the surgeon general of official secrets.
This bill was introduced by that distinguished parliamentarian in 1977, but that bill's lot was not as lucky as this one. It did not make the list of bills debated during that session of the Thirtieth Parliament. Today it has finally made it and here it is up for debate after many years. I see in fact that Mr. Baldwin has come here in order to see that the government members do not talk the bill out, and it is a pleasure to have him with us in the House today. I just hope I can do the justice to the subject that I know he would.
I say the bill is up for debate but I really do not think there is much room for debate. I believe it is worthy of speedy
passage and that tradition should be dealt a severe blow today and this private member's bill should not be talked out of existence. It should proceed through second reading and on into committee stage.
However, Mr. Speaker, I may be an optimist but I know that the government will not likely let it go. We would love to watch a member from the government benches get up and say: "We see no reason for this bill not to proceed. We feel it is in the best interests of the entire body politic." We would love to hear that and to read it tomorrow in Hansard. It would be a great pleasure to hear government spokesmen plead with us not to talk this bill into obscurity. I am a realist, however, and I doubt that will happen because the government in fact cares more about its own self-interests than the interests of the people. Government members care more about covering their behinds with official secrets acts than about giving the people of Canada the information that they have a right to see, a right which in fact should be heard.
I do not think Mr. Baldwin will be surprised when the government says, for one reason or another, that the bill cannot go forward. I will not be surprised, the party will not be surprised, in fact I doubt if any members on this side will be surprised if the bill is not sent forward by the government. All I can say, Mr. Speaker, is that we would like to see the government surprise us and let Mr. Baldwin's bill go through.
In looking at the bill we can see that it is neither lengthy nor complicated. The subject matter has received a lot of attention over the years. In fact, it was mentioned by the Secretary of State (Mr. Fox) recently as an area which needs revision. Perhaps that in fact will be the excuse for not allowing the bill to proceed today. We have heard that before. We heard it in the Thirtieth Parliament when the then minister of justice, now the minister of energy, mines and "nationalization", said it would not be long before revisions would see the light of day. That was quite a while ago. We have seen no revisions, and if we look on the Order Paper today we will see there are still no revisions by this government.
The hon. member for Nepean-Carleton (Mr. Baker), when he was the government House leader, wanted a revision of the antiquated act that was before Parliament and he realized at that time that for the freedom of information bill, which he had introduced as Bill C-15, to be meaningful legislation it had to incorporate the changes to the Official Secrets Act. In fact, he had the guts to say at that time, and I quote from Hansard of November 8, 1979:
1 should report to the hon. member that in fact there is a motion prepared. It is my hope we can deal with it at the same time as the freedom of information legislation. I hope so. I could not put that down today because, quite frankly, I have not had time to consult with the hon. member for Peace River, but I have talked to him about the actual wording of the motion. He knows the intention of the government. Now that he has raised it, and I was going to raise it later, I want the House to know that we will probably be putting that motion on the Order Paper, I guess within a day or so, so that the House can see what we have in mind.
We can see very clearly that my colleague's intentions were to get this done and to see the Official Secrets Act part of the freedom of information bill. Unfortunately, the now famous
June 4, 1981

Liberal-NDP coalition got together and decided that that was not to come about. Instead we have today economic ruin, energy collapse, and of course no revision to the Official Secrets Act. This government seems much too content to continue with its cloak and dagger syndromes of secrecy to come and say the same as the hon. member for Nepean-Carleton did. They just do not have the courage to see that kind of thing come through.
I should like to address the purpose of the bill. In fact the bill does very little; it only proposes to amend two sections. It proposes to do very little, but in fact it means a great deal. The two sections it proposes to amend are sections 3 and 4.
First I should like to look at section 3. It is amended in order more clearly to define what is an act of espionage. It would not weaken the powers of prosecuting a true agent of espionage, but it would make the section applicable to actual cases of espionage. In fact, I think this is actually the intention of section 3.
Looking briefly at section 4, the amendment to this section is to rid the statute of the unreasonable and unjustifiable clause which makes it an offence to leak information that is deemed to be anything on which the government has its name. Presently it is an offence to have this information, to hold this information, or to divulge such information, if it is felt by the state that it is "prejudicial to the interest or the security of the state".
The term is so vague and so meaningless that it has come to mean that almost any petty document or anything covered by the act in fact can constitute an offence under the act. Therefore, the purpose of the bill is to implement a few necessary amendments in order to prevent the government's discriminatory use of power through the Official Secrets Act.
Also the purpose is to prevent the exposure of members of Parliament, public servants, the press, and members of the public in general, to prosecution and possible lengthy jail terms for the most trivial exchanges of information. Another purpose is to prevent the government from using the threat of prosecution to prevent embarrassing leaks of information. We must face the fact that public servants, members of the press or even members of Parliament may be wary of discussing anything if they fear prosecution under the Official Secrets Act.
Of course, the government tells us that it would never use this power under section 4 unless it was absolutely necessary. The government indicates that the section is necessary for the good of the nation. Thank goodness the government is so concerned about our well-being! After all, if it were not for the government's concerns and the existence of section 4, many evil corrupters of state would have never been prosecuted. I am referring to evil people such as the dangerous person who endangered the entire welfare of Canada, the infamous Dr. Treu! We can thank our lucky stars that we had section 4 and the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) to ensure that he would be taken care of.
Official Secrets Act
Then there was the sinister publisher of what the Prime Minister called "that piece of garbage", The Toronto Sun. Thank heavens we had section 4. They made sure that Peter Worthington, Dr. Treu and that piece of garbage were not allowed to bother us; it was all put in its place. To think that without section 4 these people and that piece of garbage would never have been taught a lesson! They would have got away with actions which were harmful to our well-being. It does not matter that both cases were eventually acquitted by the courts! We still showed them: "Don't mess with the state or the state will mess with you"!
So we have the word of the government that section 4 will be used only when necessary. We all know just how good that word is. If we do not, perhaps we should ask Dr. Treu or Peter Worthington. I think they will tell us.
We may all breathe easy with section 4 around; we do not have to put up with undesirables who go around acting against the interests of the Privy Council. We can be saved from having to put up with the "oh, so embarrassing" situation of seeing members of the Privy Council embarrassed. No, sir. There will be no Watergate in Canada; there will be no Pentagon papers in Canada. Section 4 will see to that. There will be no uranium cartel scandal up here! Sure, we can kick and scream that something is afoul in government, but section 4 ensures that nothing is leaked. There is no chance of embarrassment for cabinet on uranium.
We must ask ourselves if it is better to have section 4, so that the government is better able to protect its honour from goof-ups and costly mistakes, or would it be better if the people of Canada were informed? Surely we would all agree that it is better for the people of Canada to be informed.
It is not a matter which is open to debate. I think the government admitted as much through the introduction of the freedom of information bill. Even the judges who sat on prosecutions under section 4, both in Canada and in the United Kingdom, with one notable exception, said that not only were the defendants not guilty, but the Official Secrets Act itself was the guilty party.
I should like to take a close look for a moment at the Peter Treu case. This will demonstrate why the act must be revised, not tomorrow, the day after or the year after, but today. Of course, Dr. Peter Treu was a matter of great discussion in the House. It was before my time, but in reading the record I found that it was all there. I think what took place is astounding.
I was amazed to see that a member of Parliament was chastised by a provincial judge for remarking in the House on the question of circumstances surrounding the prosecution and conviction. I was amazed to read the words of the minister of the Crown who answered the query of the hon. member for Halton (Mr. Jelinek) as to whether or not Treu's prosecution was linked to espionage. The reply of the minister was that Treu was not prosecuted for such deeds; yet he was prosecuted under the Official Secrets Act.

June 4, 1981
Official Secrets Act
This seems somewhat strange. Also it was amazing to discover that that prosecution, although not linked to espionage, could be tried in camera or, in other words, in secret. I thought that only happened in the days of the Star Chamber. I was amazed to discover that Dr. Treu was warned, after his prosecution and sentencing of two years in jail, that he could not discuss his trial with anyone aside from his own legal counsel. Also I discovered-and this is very important-that anyone discussing Treu's case or trial with him could be in violation of the Official Secrets Act. I am sure we could understand all of this if Treu were indeed an agent of espionage, working for the forces of evil in attempts to destroy our country. But I think it is a little hard to believe that of Peter Treu.
I should like to quote a few passages from the thus far unpublished memoirs of Mr. Baldwin. In his file Mr. Baldwin devoted two chapters to the Official Secrets Act. By reading his words into the record, I hope hon. members on all sides, especially those on the government side, might be enlightened on the seriousness of the bill and what it is trying to accomplish.
Very simply, Mr. Baldwin said:
In retrospect, as I look back in leisure, I have a feeling of anger, as well as sadness, that our system has been allowed to degenerate to such an extent that those who feel they have a grievance are liable to be intimidated as was Treu to prevent him from making complaints.
He continued further on the page:
After listening to what he said and adding to it what I had learned from his friends-
Of course, he was referring to Dr. Treu.
-plus all I had from documents I had obtained, and reading the court records, 1 ultimately pieced together a very bizarre tale. In my life in Ottawa I had learned much of the slithery, self-protective devices used by those in power to cover their flanks and protect their tracks when they felt they must do so, but this case was in a class by itself.
Then Mr. Baldwin proceeded to relate the actual circumstances surrounding the Treu case. He tells an incredible story: how the state went out of its way to persecute and prosecute a man who did not deserve such treatment. It is good reading. When it is published I hope all hon. members of the House will consider reading it, because all of us can learn something about ourselves from it.
On the actual charges which Treu faced, which were the possession of classified material and that his storage of those materials was somehow endangering the security of the state, Mr. Baldwin had this to say, which I think is relevant to the matter:
How did these ridiculous charges come to be laid? On whose advice? What documents were produced to the Attorney General to persuade him that the safety of the realm depended on the prosecution of this man on such trumped up and silly charges? I'm afraid these and many other related questions may never be answered unless we get a freedom of information law which will permit a court in the fullness of time to approve the disclosure of such facts which could provide the answers.
Thus we see the connection between the Official Secrets Act and the Freedom of Information Act, albeit in a slightly different way. Then Mr. Baldwin said:
The case became something of a cause celebre, and focused much attention on the Official Secrets Act, so much that in spite of opposition in certain government quarters it was pretty well conceded that for there to be a useful freedom of information law, there has to be radical surgery on the Official Secrets Act in general, and section 4 in particular.
Here it is, Mr. Speaker. Bill C-411 has come back to haunt the government as Bill C-246, with its ghost looking down from above. We cannot escape it this time. The time has come to answer to the people of Canada. If this government is truly sincere about freedom of information, about the right of the people of Canada to have and to hold information which rightfully belongs to them, then we must let this bill proceed. It is surgery which is needed. Let the government spokesman rise to close the incision which was opened by my predecessor. I hope he will do that.
It was not long ago that I rose in my place to give my first speech, my maiden speech, in this House. At that time I was speaking on a motion to refer the Official Secrets Act to committee. The government refused this simple request, even though an identical motion, or an almost identical one except that it was toned down to meet the expected objections of the government, was agreed to one year earlier when the present government was in opposition. I still wonder why they changed their mind. The reason given by the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Labour (Mr. Desmarais) was as follows:
The wording of the motion is quite wrong. It prejudices the work of the standing committee. I also believe that this is not a suitable time to refer the Official Secrets Act to a standing committee of this House.
The reason he felt that the timing was wrong was, I believe, that the McDonald commission had yet to release its final report. I do not think that excuse holds water for two reasons. First, the McDonald commission released an interim report which was specifically on official secrets and security matters. I wonder if the hon. member for Dollard read that report. In speaking to my motion, in October of last year he said:
The McDonald commission has been examining the policies and practices which now apply to the protection of the security of Canada-
Later on he said:
But we have yet to receive a comprehensive report from the commission of inquiry on matters of security policy-
I do not think the hon. member could have read the interim report. It is lengthy, very comprehensive and, in fact, contains many recommendations.
This brings me to my second argument against his objections of October last, which is the fact that the McDonald commission did not do a truly non-partisan job on the matter and the report should be viewed in that light. This can be exemplified through another quote from Mr. Baldwin's memoirs, which are receiving much attention today. Of the commission's interim report he said the following:
In a portion of this report so worded as to make it clear that only the government side has been heard, special mention of the Treu case was made and it was suggested other charges could have been laid on which he could have been convicted but the government couldn't find witnesses! This is exactly the same sort of vague statement which had been relayed to me and to members of the press gallery in an attempt to persuade us to lay off this case and leave Treu to
June 4, 1981

the government's tender mercies. This should never have been said! In effect it constituted a trial of Dr. Treu on a charge never laid against him, and on which he was never called to defend, and to which he could not effectively reply, especially with the wide publicity given to the report.
The parliamentary secretary's other reason for refusing to allow the motion of last October to go through-which I again remind him he and his party had agreed to unanimously and defended with such fortitude before-was that the motion prejudiced the committee's work. That is nonsense. If it was so prejudiced, why did he vote for it the time before? Is his party of such hypocritical nature that it believes his excuse washes down with a bit of governmental backwash? I do not want to hear those excuses today. We want the government to come clean, either to say that it likes the Official Secrets Act the way it is-that is, firmly entrenched in the secret passageways of governmental administration-or, if it means what it says, that it should come clean and let this bill go through.
Failing this, there is still one other alternative, and that is to lay its own bill on the table today. I think the government has one ready, but I do not think it knows if it wants it. The government may think that it can hoodwink the public with a watered down freedom of information bill and say that it is enough. I know what the government will say. Someone from the government side will probably get up and say that the timing is bad. He will say that Bill C-246 is not right and that the government will not let it proceed. The government will not let the people go. It could not wrestle inflation to the ground, so it will be content to wrestle the people of Canada to the ground.
I ended my speech on this subject last October with a favourite quotation which my predecessor uses on many occasions. It is from the Bible. I think that it is very timely and pertinent to the particular piece of legislation we are debating today. Once again I would like to close with that quotation and say to the government: "The truth shall set you free".
Hear, hear!

speakeroldname: Mr. Ron Irwin (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Justice and Minister of State for Social Development):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State for Social Development
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I commend the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Cooper) for once again bringing this very important topic to the attention of the House.
The Official Secrets Act was passed in 1939. Prior to that time the legislation concerning this area was really an English statute which we had adopted in 1911. There were very minor changes to it in 1950, 1967, 1970 and 1972. Over one half of the prosecutions under the act were as a result of the defection of Igor Gouzenko in 1946. At that time he tried to set up a network of spies in Canada.
The hon. member for Peace River is trying to make much of the amount of activity there has been under this act since then. As the hon. member knows, there has not been much activity. There have been only four cases prosecuted under the act. There was the Biernacki case in 1961, the Featherstone case in 1967, the Treu case in 1978 and The Toronto Sun case last year.
Official Secrets Act
As far as Biernacki goes, he was a Polish landed immigrant who tried to set up a spy network in Canada. He was acquitted, and in the words of the learned trial judge the information was "insignificant, worthless public information".
As far as the Featherstone case goes, we were lucky with him. He was sending charts of marine wreckage to the Russians, I believe it was. Apparently submarines can hide behind this wreckage and go undetected by radar. This was an open and closed case and Featherstone received a two and a half year sentence.
All members of the House are familiar with the Treu case.
As far as The Toronto Sun is concerned, they had an alleged top secret report which showed suspected Russian spy activity in Canada. The editor of the paper was acquitted because the document no longer, if ever, was secret.
So, as I have outlined, there really has not been that much activity under the Official Secrets Act. This sometimes makes me wonder whether we are, perhaps, allowing too many of our state secrets to escape to the enemies of Canada-and we have several, economic and otherwise-without recourse. It is important that we discuss the Official Secrets Act, but it is also important that we not say that it is part and parcel of what is going on in a parliamentary committee. Surely the hon. member would agree that we must have some sanctions against those who sell our state secrets or give our state secrets to foreign powers, allowing them to become threats to our economy and to our nation as a whole.
We must decide-and we are-how broad or narrow the access to information legislation should be. We must also decide how broad or narrow the Official Secrets Act should be. Are we making it more difficult under the access to information legislation for the public, members of the opposition and members of Parliament to obtain information? Are the Prime Minister's guidelines sufficient if they are adhered to?
The other day a member of the opposition said that perhaps we should have a preamble to the access to information legislation which basically incorporates the concept which the Prime Minister was alluding to last April when he established five simple guidelines. We must decide-and we have discussed this before in the House-whether to take the espionage section out of the Official Secrets Act and place it in the Criminal Code, with a proper sentence. We must decide whether to take the unintentional or the leakage sections out of the Official Secrets Act and place them in special legislation, and repeal the present act.
Basically, all I have heard today is the same rhetoric I heard in earlier discussions. There has been nothing in any concrete form. There have been many allusions to measures we have taken, but more to the state of the economy, the energy plan and the Constitution.
If we are to discuss access to information and the Official Secrets Act, then let us discuss them. Let us not enter into other topics of discussion. It is important that members of Parliament understand what must be done and what we are doing under access to information legislation and under the
10276

June 4, 1981
Official Secrets Act
Official Secrets Act. It is also important that bureaucrats understand what is being done and, finally, that the public also understands.
I think that the hon. member opposite does not understand the act because his definition deals with the security of Canada. Even members of his own party have criticized that definition in this House, yet he proposes it in his bill today. I agree with those members of his party who believe that by putting that forward he may be extending the scope of the legislation that narrows the bill. I do not think he intends that, but that is exactly what members of his party are saying. I would not support what he is saying even if he extended the definition.
The explanatory note to the bill reads as follows:
This bill is necessary for freedom of information to become a meaningful piece of legislation. Unless amended, the Official Secrets Act and the access to information act will contradict each other.
What is the contradiction, Mr. Speaker? First we have to see if there is a conflict, and if there is, whether it is contradictory.
The access to information act provides for access to records. Clause 4 of the bill defines the word "record" very broadly, as follows:
-includes any correspondence, memorandum, book, plan, map, drawing, diagram, pictorial or graphic work, photograph, film, microform, sound recording, videotape, machine readable record, and any other documentary materials, regardless of physical form or characteristics, and any copy thereof;
Section 4 provides for a number of limited, narrowly-defined exemptions. Under the access to information act the civil servant who issues the information requested, is protected if he follows a certain pattern of notice. This is not the case under the Official Secrets Act; something is either an official secret or it is not.
Clause 71 of the access to information act protects the public servant. It reads as follows:
Notwithstanding any other acts of Parliament, no civil or criminal proceedings lie against the head of any government institution, or against any person acting on behalf or under the direction of the head of a government institution, and no proceedings lie against the Crown, for the disclosure in good faith of any record or any part of a record pursuant to this act, or for any consequences that flow from such disclosure, or for the failure to give any notice required under this act, if reasonable care is taken to given the required notice.
We have to remember that we are dealing with records under the access to information act. I would ask the hon. member to read Section 3(1) of the Official Secrets Act to see if there is a conflict. It reads as follows:
Every person is guilty of an offence under this act who, for any purpose prejudicial to the safety or interests of the state,
(a)	approaches, inspects, passes over, or is in the neighbourhood of, or enters
any prohibited place;
There is no conflict between that section and the access to information act which is being examined in committee. The section continues:
(b)	makes any sketch, plan, model or note that is calculated to be or might be
or is intended to be directly or indirectly useful to a foreign power;
Again, there is no conflict between to the access to information act and the Official Secrets Act. Subsection (c) may have some relevance. It reads as follows:
(c)	obtains, collects, records, or publishes, or communicates to any other person any secret official code word, or pass word, or any sketch, plan, model, article, or note, or other document or information that is calculated to be or might be or is intended to be directly or indirectly useful to a foreign power.
There might be some relevance at first blush but I assume no one in this House would want to release state secrets, as password or a code word, under the access to information act, that would be useful to a foreign power.
Moving to Section 4, only 4(1 )(a) and 4(4)(b) have any relevance to the disclosure of government information.
Section 4(1 )(a), makes it an offence for an individual to disclose information to any " ... person, other than a person to whom he is authorized to communicate with, or a person to whom it is in the interest of the State his duty to communicate it;".
This would not, of course, conflict with the access legislation which authorizes disclosure of information to the public in general.
In Section 4(4)(b), the only relevant provision makes it an offence if someone "allows any other person to have possession of any official document issued for his use alone, or communicates any secret official code word or pass word so issued, or, without lawful authority or excuse-".
Again, the same argument can be made as in relation to paragraph 4(1 )(a), that this is overridden by the authorization provided by the access legislation.
I believe there is need for an overhaul of the Official Secrets Act and I shall deal with that later, but I cannot agree with the proposition put forward by my hon. friend. However, I believe that the approach proposed by the bill is quite inappropriate and I do not accept the argument that we do not have time to do a proper review of the act.
As I have explained, I do not accept the position that the Official Secrets Act must be revised in this piecemeal fashion in order to avoid conflict with the access to information act. 1 think there is a proper time for debate on the access to information bill and that is when it comes out of committee. We are pressing to have it out of committee, back in the House and passed before the summer recess. If that does not happen, the official opposition and perhaps the NDP will be to blame.
In the new bill there are seven pages of government entities in which the public will have access to information. In certain entities there will not be that same openness. These could be put into the competitive group, first, and then into the group where we have a small interest. We do not think it is fair that a company which competes with a government company should have an unfair advantage, and we do not think it is fair that other companies competing with government companies, do not have the same cost in keeping up with the access to information act. We have left alone the entities in which the government has only a small interest, but some of them may be brought in. For instance, the Canadian Development Cor-
June 4, 1981

poration is not included, nor is a motel in the maritimes in which the government has a small interest.
With regard to environmental information that has been requested, it is now the objective case that is being used. Due to the recent amendment, the minister will no longer be able to say, on a subjective basis, "I think you should not have access to this environmental testing information." An object test will be used and if the applicant for the information is not satisfied, he can apply to the court.
1 should like to quote from an article which appeared in The Globe and Mail on June 3 by Robert Sheppard as follows:
The new tack is part of a series of amendments Secretary of State Francis Fox announced yesterday that he is prepared to accept when the bill comes up for final reading.
It represents a marked departure from the first draft (not to mention briefs by the Canadian business community), which would have allowed the withholding of financial or technical information supplied the government in confidence by private firms on the grounds that to allow access to such information could result in financial loss or prejudice competitive positions.
I only quote from The Globe and Mail because, as everyone knows, it is probably our most severe critic. I think that is a favourable comment.
To go back to my other point, 1 think the Prime Minister's guidelines of April of last year are excellent if their spirit is followed. We have no access to information, and we still do not have the legislation. In April of last year, the Right Hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) set five guidelines for all civil servants. The first guideline sets out that part of their duties is to discuss the goings on of government with the public and people who want access to information. Under the second guideline it is stated that public servants must be frank in their discussions. I will not read all the guidelines because they have been circulated. But under the third guideline it is stated that public servants are not to speculate on policy deliberations or future policy decisions. Under the fourth guideline it is stated that it is normal for public servants to be quoted by name and the individual can be interviewed for radio and television as well as for the print media.
The fifth guideline gives me the most problem. It probably gives the bureaucracy the most problem also. It reads:
These guidelines cannot and do not authorize the disclosure of information which is specifically prohibited by law. Public employees acting in good faith under these guidelines will not be considered as having violated their oaths of secrecy.
We are hoping that the seven pages in the access to information bill listing the entities which are mentioned and the guidelines which have been set down will make it much clearer to the bureaucracy and public servants just where their duties lie vis-a-vis the public, without having to worry about being chastised by their superiors, the deputy minister or the minister.
In the four minutes I have remaining I shall discuss parts of the Official Secrets Act that I hope will be amended in the near future.
Official Secrets Act
Under the penalty section, which is Section 15, it is now left to the discretion of the Crown attorney, who takes the case, or the ministry of justice as to whether they should proceed summarily or by way of indictment. If the Crown proceeds by way of indictment, the maximum term is 14 years. If the Crown proceeds summarily, the penalty is $500, 12 months, or both. That is under Section 3 or Section 4 of the Official Secrets Act. In my opinion, it gives too much discretion to the individual Crown attorney. One responsible commission suggested that in relation to espionage, the maximum term be life. As far as the intentional and unintentional leakage is concerned, that same commission suggested the maximum term be six years and the discretion of indictable or summary process be taken away from individual Crown attorneys.
As far as presumption is concerned, perhaps the charter of rights will say, when it is passed, hopefully, by the fall of this year, that everyone who is presumed innocent before the law can challenge the presumption that we have passed as a federal government under the Official Secrets Act.
There is an excellent article by Mr. M. L. Friedland of the University of Toronto who reported to the McDonald commission. This article is entitled "National Security: The Legal Dimensions". In it he goes through the different presumptions. They really are archaic and, I think, dangerous. To give an example, if presumptions A and B are true, therefore, C and D are true. These are presumed true without having to be proven or called in evidence. Not only are there presumptions, there are double presumptions, and that is probably the worst example in any federal act of the presumption of innocence being taken away.
There is no right to a trial by jury under the Official Secrets Act. I think there should be a right to a jury. A jury could be an optional choice, as the McDonald commission suggested. In other words, the accused could ask for it. Second, the onus is on the crown, namely the government, and it must show by trial that it would not be in the best interests of the country to have a jury. If there is any doubt though, that doubt should go to the accused. Finally, the jury should be sworn to secrecy. The procedure is, therefore possible.
I think we can get carried away with freedom of information. There is a responsibility for government to handle the massive amount of information that we accumulate from the public, usually because it is mandatory.
In England in 1972 the Franks report was issued. It is very relevant to our situation because our legislation is based on the English legislation. It reads:
We have so far indicated these wider issues in the most general terms. But they can be more simply expressed. Even a democratic government requires a measure of secrecy for some of its functions, as a means whereby it can better carry out its duties on behalf of the people. Among the primary tasks of government are the defence of the nation from external threats, the maintenance of relations with the rest of the world and the preservation of law and order.
Once again I commend the hon. member for bringing this matter to the House. But I would think that at this stage as a government we have proceeded closer to reality than ever before in the history of our country. Very shortly we will have

Official Secrets Act
an access to information act that, in the words of many witnesses who came before the parliamentary committee, is much superior to the U.S. model from which we derived the original concept. I am very proud of it. I am very proud that we, as a government, are putting it forward. I think it is unjust criticism to suggest that we are doing nothing. It is always in the best interests of the government, because it is easier, not to give the public information. We are giving the public that information. We are standing on that bill and I hope that in the fall the hon. member will acknowledge that something is being done.

Mr. Speaker, first I shall say a few words in support of the bill presented by the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Cooper) and to commend him for continuing in the tradition of his predecessor, Ged Baldwin, who distinguished himself not only in this area of the Official Secrets Act and by pointing out to Canadians the terrible manner in which the Peter Treu trial was conducted but also for his outstanding work in the area of freedom of information legislation. As I say, I must express my gratitude to the hon. member for bringing this important subject before Parliament today.
Just a few moments ago I came from the hearings of the justice committee dealing with freedom of information legislation and access to information legislation. I think it should be stated very clearly that there are a number of major flaws in that legislation including, among others, that there is a transitional period which renders largely ineffective the provisions for a review, presently contained in the bill. Unless that transitional provision is changed and unless there are certain other changes made to sections of that bill which are so central to the issue, we will have great difficulty in recognizing it as being a bill which moves us forward in the area of access to information.
The hon. member for Sault Ste. Marie (Mr. Irwin) stated that many witnesses who appeared before the committee indicated that the bill was superior to the American bill. I attended those hearings, and I would challenge the hon. member to indicate any witness who appeared before that committee, whether representatives of the Canadian Bar Association, representatives of access, representatives of the consumer association or any other witnesses, who stated that this bill was in any way superior in its exemptions, or in any other way, to the U.S. legislation. I think the Minister of Justice (Mr. Chretien) has been listening to departmental officials, because he certainly was not listening to the witnesses who appeared before our committee.
We are dealing here with a proposal by the hon. member for Peace River to get rid of a bill which is surely an anachronism and one of the most archaic bills presently on the statute books of Canada. Frankly, it is a bill which tends to bring into disrepute the administration of justice generally in this country.
The McDonald commission purportedly examined the effects of the Official Secrets Act. In so doing, it vilified, in a manner which I found shocking, the reputation of Peter Treu.
He was not on trial before the McDonald commission, and yet that commission saw fit to cast very serious aspersions on his activities. I might say, if that is any indication of the calibre of report which the commission will be submitting to the Government of Canada, then the taxpayers of Canada have had some $10 million of their money wasted.
Why is it essential that this motion be supported? Primarily because we have a government in Canada which is wedded to a concept of secrecy. The government suggests that freedom of information is being brought in. Indeed, all parties in this House support the principle of freedom of information legislation. However, the bill leaves a great deal to be desired. There are still far too many statutes which contain secrecy provisions. The most odious of all of those statutes is the Official Secrets Act.
Nothing is being done by this government to remove the sweeping sanctions which exist under the provisions of the Official Secrets Act for disclosure of information, in some cases trivial information. Under the ambit of section 4 of the Official Secrets Act, it is an offence to disclose any information, no matter how minor. That flies in the face of the government's supposed commitment to open access to information.
There have been many recommendations for changes to the bill. The hon. member for Sault Ste. Marie pointed out some of the concerns. What we are looking for on the part of this government is an indication that they are at least serious about having this matter studied. That is all that is being asked for, that the justice committee have an opportunity to examine the defects in the bill, which are admitted by members from the other side. For example, the right to trial by jury, which is surely fundamental, is denied to those persons being prosecuted under the Official Secrets Act, as well as the fact that the sanction of the criminal law in its full force applies to activities to which surely it should not apply in this day and age. As the hon. member for Peace River indicated, there are many other weaknesses in the bill.
What we suggest is very much along the lines suggested by the Canadian Civil Liberties Association in their excellent presentation to the McDonald commission, focusing particularly on section 4 of the Official Secrets Act. They urge that the test that should be applied is one of a reasonable expectation of serious injury to the physical safety and defence of Canada, but beyond that the criminal sanction should not apply to the unauthorized disclosure of government information and that certainly that criminal sanction should not apply to those who may receive that information, whether it be in the press, Parliament or elsewhere.
They urge a number of safeguards, even within the range of safety and defence secrets, including the fact that the material must not have previously entered the public realm, or the fact that the accused knew or had reasonable ground to believe that the material at issue fell into the requisite category or that the document in question was improperly classified. The offence of
June 4, 1981

receiving such information should be removed from the statute books.
As I indicated, some of the safeguards are lacking now, such as the absence of the right to trial by jury, the Draconian penalties in many cases, and the failure of the bill to accord the right to a public trial. These are the kinds of things this motion urges be changed.
We welcome the motion. We urge the government to accept the very reasonable suggestion that this bill, which has been condemned so roundly by many groups going back to the 1969 McDonald commission and a similar bill which was thoroughly condemned by the Franks committee in Britain, be studied to bring our legislation into the twentieth century.
If the government is serious about its commitment to freedom of information-a commitment given, we suspect, because of the weakness of their bill on access to information-hand in hand with that legislation must come the obligation of the government to overhaul substantially this archaic piece of legislation, the Official Secrets Act, so that the government is not giving with one hand and taking away with the other.
In conclusion, we strongly support this motion. I commend the hon. member for Peace River for once again drawing the attention of Parliament to the importance of this subject matter. I sincerely hope the government will see fit to support the motion.

Mr. Speaker, I will only say a few words on this so that there will be time left to vote on it. The hon. member for Sault Ste. Marie (Mr. Irwin) said that there are some shortcomings in the bill. If that is so, it is all the more reason why it should be sent to committee where any shortcomings can be corrected. There is no reason to talk out a bill because it has one or two shortcomings. It is the job of the committee to find if there are any and, if so, to correct them.
There are two things the Official Secrets Act should not do. This bill will correct that. If necessary, it will be even further corrected by the committee. First, it should not be used to hide information. There are grave suspicions today that the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) is using the bill to hide information in connection with the uranium cartel. It should not be a case of hiding information to which the public is entitled. The Official Secrets Act is to stop information which, if made public, would endanger the country, not to hide information from the people in order to protect the government. That is very important.
Second, this bill should not be used to threaten the citizens of Canada. There have been threats against a number of people, including a bus driver and Peter Treu. If something improper is done, a charge should be laid. There should be none of this threat business. The bill uses such loose language as "is calculated to be". That is like using the word "deemed" in the Income Tax Act. You can deem this and deem that. Here we are calculating. There should be proof before someone is charged under the Official Secrets Act.

Mr. Speaker, I have great pleasure tonight and some agitation in speaking to motion No. 4 because it deals with a tax that I think should never be allowed in a democratic country.
In dealing with indexation of tax I want to go back to the basis of British liberty. Hon. members who know their history will know that King John had the habit of demanding taxation from his people, to the extent that his people just could not afford to pay. He was ruining his country, and even though it was a feudal system at the time, the demands were so great that the people just could not stand the burden. Consequently, on June 15, 1215, when King John returned from a trip, a group of English people were there to meet him. After discussion, they forced King John to sign what has become known as the Magna Carta, or the Magna Charter. Throughout the world, and especially throughout the British World, 1215 at Runnymede was the time when the fundamental bases of the rights of people were established.
I want to deal with just one aspect of that charter. The great council forced King John to agree that when financial aid was required by the Crown and the Crown wanted an additional amount, the Crown could not levy taxes on barons or on estates. Rather, the great council had to be called together, and the great council would determine how much the king would receive. King John did not sign the Magna Carta readily, but he had to sign it. The great council of that day made certain rules and regulations so that the many provisions of the Magna Carta could be enforced. The Magna Carta of Runnymede of June 15, 1215 contained the basic rights certainly of the British people and probably of people who love freedom all over the world. It was a great charter of English personal and political liberty which was obtained from King John. There were 61 or 63 sections of the charter, but the meaning of the charter could be summed up by the term "no taxation without representation". I think that is the real
history of the success of democracy. The right to levy taxes without representation was taken from the king.
Parliaments and governments evolved, and when governments wished to levy taxation, that was not permitted without representations from the people. Parliament had to be called annually so that those representations could be heard. That was the only control over governments wanting to increase taxation. They had to bring such matters before the representatives of the people so that they could be debated. That practice, of course, has carried on to this day.
Today there is a necessity to call Parliament and every legislature in Canada at least once a year, not necessarily to pass laws, although that is done, but to make sure governments have money to operate and to make sure representations are heard before taxes are increased. This does not involve taxation already in place, but it does affect proposed tax increases. Any proposed tax increase must be dealt with in that way.
Motion No. 4 deals with clause 1 lines 1 to 23 at page 4. It is proposed that there be an arrangement whereby it will not be necessary to have representation with respect to increased taxation. I want to emphasize that. If that indexation of taxation goes through respecting the items to which it is to apply, it will no longer be necessary to call the representatives of the people together. It will not be necessary to include this matter in budgets. It will not be necessary to have it carried in the press. It will simply be done by the government without hearing representations from the representatives of the people. This government wants to do the same thing for which King John was called to account. It wants to impose taxation without representation. In the days of King John, any additional levies on the people had to be discussed with the great council.
I would like to deal with indexing for a moment. This party has made indexing of pensions part and parcel of our policy. Hundreds of people across the country agree with that policy. I remember attending a forum in 1979. All candidates were asked what they would do about indexing pensions. It was easy for me to answer. When a pensioner secures a pension, that pension is to pay for his food, clothing and shelter. Then, if food prices, rents or clothing prices increase, how can a pensioner meet those costs with the pension he was granted before those increased costs came into play?
Indexing adds something. Perhaps it is not enough, but it adds something to the amount of a pension so that the pensioner can meet increased costs which arise through no fault of his own. Those costs may rise because of inflation, because of taxation or because of any of several other causes. Indexed pensions give pensioners something additional with which to meet those increased costs.
I come now to what happens when taxation is indexed. The very reverse happens. Pensions which are indexed increase to meet increased costs. That is very helpful, but when there are unusual price increases such as increases in the price of heating oil, gasoline or rents, even indexed pensions are not sufficient. It becomes very difficult for pensioners to survive. However, when we index taxation as well, we aggravate the
June 4, 1981

problem. Taxes are a charge on the individual, and pensioners and veterans are included with everyone else. When we increase taxes, we take away from pensioners and veterans part of what they need for a living. When additional taxation is levied, that increases the cost of goods. Consumers must pay increased costs for goods plus increased taxes. That is what motion No. 4 is all about. I refer here to subclause (6). That is what 1 claim is contrary to the very spirit of British law. It is taxation without representation.
I want to emphasize that, Mr. Speaker, because 1 believe that the Ontario legislature and now the House of Commons are embarking on a plan of taxation that cannot be authorized in a democracy. If we authorize it, we are defying the very basis of the Magna Carta. We are saying to the government: "Go ahead and increase taxes without representation." That is neither sound nor right, and I violently oppose the inclusion of indexing of taxes in this bill. Taxes are a charge on the individual and when they are increased without even a debate, without the press carrying the story, without any chance of dealing with it at all, that is wrong. Whether or not the House of Commons or the legislatures are able to reduce the normal tax, at least it is debated and people have a chance to prepare for the increased deductions from their pensions or wages.

Mr. Speaker, there is a place for philosophy and respect for the principles of government, but there is no place for either in the hands of the government of this day. I am rather surprised that my highly respected friend, the hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Taylor) would expect that this government would consider that justice had anything to do with taxation and its procedures.
During report stage of Bill C-57 a great many remarks were made which related somewhat to the excise tax on a wide range of products and services. In general terms, this legislation could not be called anything but repugnant.
The fact that it will increase government revenues is contrary to the election promises of this government, but promises are only to be made during campaigns and not during government, according to this one. That is not the primary source of objection, but rather it is the scope of changes that this bill will effect on the revenue-gathering process that is so utterly objectionable. Taken in its entirety, this document emphasizes the fact that the government is virtually bankrupt. It is going to ask the taxpayer to bail it out. Bill C-57 is an excessive money grab, and it is when one scrutinizes the bill clause by clause, that one discovers the truly insidious nature of this revenue grab.
While I only have time today to speak on a few problems that this bill presents, I want to make it perfectly clear that there are a great many more sections of this bill that concern me. I am confident that my colleagues on this side of the House will be making full and adequate representations on these further clauses on behalf of taxpayers as did the previous speaker.
A number of people have made representations with regard to the portion of Bill C-57 that imposes indexed excise taxes on alcoholic beverages. The Canadian Brewers Association, the Canadian Association of Provincial Liquor Commissions, and
Excise Tax
Ontario winemakers have made appeals to many members of this House for changes in this portion of the legislation.
Particularly upsetting to these groups has been the proposed indexation of these excise taxes to the consumer price index. Objections to this proposed practice have been both philosophical and practical in nature. Let me make it quite clear that while no one objects to the federal government's right to collect revenue from the sale of alcoholic beverages, it is the fashion in which it proposes to do so that has thrown this industry into a turmoil, and people who respect democratic government into a state of fright.
For myself, I have some trouble with the way in which it abrogates the right of Parliament to consider appropriation bills. If this measure is in fact accepted-and I am repeating what others have said, but it bears repeating-it will no longer be necessary for the minister to stand up in the House when presenting the budget, and say "I am going to change the excise taxes on alcoholic beverages by a specific amount." He no longer has to come before Parliament; he no longer announces to the people that the tax rate is going up. That is the principle of government and has been since King John, since the Magna Carta and since Runnymede. That is the principle of democratic government as we have known it. To me it is just another example on the long list of affronts that those opposite have made to the rights of Parliamentarians- taxation without announcement, taxation with deceitful representation.
As well, it joins the growing list of ways in which the government is trying to deceive the Canadian public on matters of revenue gathering. Some would argue that any provincial sales tax is, in fact, an indexed tax, and while to a limited degree that is true, a provincial sales tax does not have the same effect as would this proposed indexed excise tax.
In order to make this point more clearly, let me review the fashion in which this indexed tax will be administered. Prior to the introduction of this budget, excise taxes on alcoholic spirits were at a fixed level of $17.15 per proof gallon. Prior to April 1980, the level was $16.25 per proof gallon, and had been at that level for a number of years. With its excessive requirements for revenue, the government decided that alcoholic beverages was an area in which taxation was not keeping pace with the need for revenue. Therefore, in Bill C-57, it proposed a change whereby the amount of excise tax collected would be indexed to the alcoholic subgroup of the consumer price index. It was proposed that the taxes be adjusted quarterly.
With that brief understanding of the way in which the tax would be administered, one can quickly see that the tax would generate its own increases. An increase in the excise tax prompts an increase in the price of alcohol, which in turn moves the consumer price index up, which prompts an increase in the excise tax. The provincial sales tax may generate further revenues when there is a jump in the consumer price index, but the tax itself, however, does not generate its own increase, as would be the case with this proposal. It is pyramiding the impact of the indexing of a tax. The indexation of excise taxes

on alcoholic beverages not only escalates inflation, but it gives the government an overwhelming interest in inflation. It puts the government in conflict with its own policy because the higher the price, the greater the revenue, the more it spends. And they coax people into thinking it is a good government!
Now what of other objections that have been raised against this proposal. One is that it would create inequalities between various product types in the industry. The Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) said in his speech that he was particularly sensitive to changes in the weight of taxation between the various products. However, this is not borne out in this particular part of the bill. It is widely known that consumers have only a certain portion of their disposable income to spend on any particular facet of their livelihood.
If a bottle of beer costs SI, and a mixed drink costs $2, then it is obvious that the consumer will take more of the lower priced product. However, because changes in excise taxes will be indexed to a percentage change in the alcoholic subgroup of the CPI, a producer of a lower priced product is able to gain a further competitive edge over those of higher priced products simply by raising the price of his product. That is to say, if the price of a bottle of beer goes to $1.10, then the percentage change in the excise tax would be felt more heavily by those selling the higher priced product. If one were to speculate, one would expect that a failure of the grape crop in Italy would give a tremendous advantage to domestic wine producers in that year. On the other hand, the price of imported wines from Italy would greatly increase, and domestic producers would gain a distinct advantage. That is the way it would appear.
However, because of the fact that the increased price of foreign wine would reflect in the consumer price index and thus alter the excise tax, there would be an impact on domestic producers who would lose a proportion of their competitive advantage because the increment of tax would take hold. It is also true that rampant inflation in another country would have an across-the-board effect on the prices of alcohol in this country. The fluctuations in currency, exchange rates, etc, would not simply affect the imported product; they would affect all products that are sold when measured to the CPI.
One need not go abroad, however, to see the awful effects of this legislation. Ontario, for instance, by its very size, controls a very large portion of the sales of alcohol in this country. If the government in Ontario decided to alter the tax it collects on the sale of alcohol, then that would have a major impact on the CPI and, in turn, it would have an across-the-board effect on tax, and thus on prices all across the country. An increase of price in Ontario would have a definite and dramatic effect on the alcoholic subgroup on the CPI. In short, price mark-up in any jurisdiction could cause a price mark-up in every jurisdiction.
Looking at this whole question from an entirely practical point of view, the government may in fact be cutting off its nose to spite its face. Everyone is aware of the fact that there is a point beyond which no product can be taxed. That is to
say, taxation beyond a certain point will result in diminishing returns by virtue of a decrease in sales. I am afraid that that might just be the case in this instance. There is another factor. When the price of any product gets too high, no matter what the control, people may find ways and means to produce a product which is beyond the tax arm of the government.
Because of our recent economic hard time, the volume of sales in the alcoholic beverage groups is increasing only about 2 per cent a year. This is due strictly to the dollars and cents involved, and it has occurred during a time when excise tax remained largely unchanged. In 1977, the federal excise tax on alcoholic spirit was, as I mentioned earlier, $16.25 a proof gallon. Last April it changed to $17.50 a proof gallon, an increase of 90 cents. This change was made in the normal way of announcing a tax increment and it was voted upon in this House. The tax remained at that level until the introduction of the last budget.
By way of illustration, had the excise tax on alcoholic beverages been indexed to changes in the alcoholic subgroup of the CPI over the same period of years, the tax would have stood at $20.77 prior to the introduction of this budget. Rather than a 90-cent increase over a three-year period, there would have been a $4.50 increase which, in itself, would have constituted a 500 per cent increase in federal excise tax rates. That is how it multiplies. It feeds upon itself when aided by inflation. If one acknowledges that the growth rate in sales stood at 2 per cent when there was a 90-cent increase, one can only wonder to what level sales would have fallen had that figure been increased 500 per cent. I wonder, just as an aside, how many bootleggers we might have had in this country by this time.
One can clearly see from this that it will not require a very long period of time before the government finds its revenues declining as a result of these numerous and dramatic changes in the excise tax rate levied on alcoholic beverages. I have no sympathy in particular with either the tobacco industry or the alcohol industry. I am probably one of the heavier users of tobacco in this House. I am not proud of it, but I guess I am the victim of my own weakness. But the alcohol part of it does not bother me that much.

When we are elected to come here on behalf of our constituents, we do the best that we can to scrutinize government spending so that it is spent in the most desirable way possible.
That also has some implications with regard to how the money is to be raised. If this bill is passed without the amendment, we will have some very grave concerns in the future about how money is to be raised in the sense that it can be raised automatically without any regard for the concerns of members of this House and, therefore, the concerns of our constituents.
Something else to bear in mind in terms of treasury bills is that those responsible for initiating the spending of money are the members of the cabinet, of which there are roughly 32. If you divide $60 billion by 32, each cabinet minister is responsible for something like $2 billion of spending. That is a very sobering thought. When you look down the benches of the cabinet and think that each of those individuals is responsible for something like $2 billion of Canadian tax money, you get the willies, as should every taxpayer in Canada. To entrust the spending of $2 billion, as an average figure, to each cabinet minister is, I repeat, a very sobering thought.

(a) aggregating the Alcoholic Beverages Subgroups or the Tobacco Products and Smokers' Supplies Subgroup of the Consumer Price Index, as the case may be, as published by Statistics Canada under the authority of the Statistics Act-
What we are talking about is the consumer price index and how it is to be used as a method of indexing the taxes in the subgroup referred to in that clause of the bill. I have some problems with the consumer price index. That is a topic that could be discussed at length on another occasion.
Very briefly, when we talk about a basket of goods as being static, that basket does not change as prices change. We assume that once a consumer buys the goods in that basket, he will continue to buy those items in the same quantity no matter what the price may be. We want to tie the index to something the validity of which I question. It goes on to say that this may be:
-adjusted or altered in such manner as the Governor in Council may, by regulation, prescribe, for each month in that period-
That means the governor in council, the cabinet, may decide that the consumer price index is not valid for purposes of this indexing procedure. It may change it at will without any reference back to the House of Commons. This is a deplorable type of clause to put in a bill. It further removes the accountability of the government through the elected members of Parliament to the citizens of this country who pay the tax.
As was pointed out by other speakers, you end up with a pyramid situation where you have tax on tax on tax. Let me give an example. An increase in the price of bread may come about as a result of an increase in the price of flour, presumably as a result of an increase in the price of wheat to the farmer. That could cause an increase in the consumer price index and therefore an increase in this tax. As the consumer price index goes up, the tax goes up, which could cause the consumer price index to go up again. You get a snowballing effect. It keeps going faster and faster. That is similar to the insatiable appetite this government has for money. It is in a frantic search for funds. When looking around for places to derive revenue, it starts looking at such things as are mentioned in this bill.
That, very briefly, is my concern. I do not want to take too much of the time of the House. Let me close by making the observation that this is a very large bill, 116 pages long with 132 clauses. It is very complicated in terms of the average Canadian trying to understand how our taxation system works.
When it becomes difficult for the average Canadian to understand how the taxation system works, he loses respect for law and order in this country. That is a very serious implication which can be drawn from this bill. I do not know how anyone going through this bill can really understand the total implications of what we are discussing this evening. Therefore, it is incumbent upon us to take as much time as we require to look at each clause so that we as legislators can do the best job we can on behalf of those who sent us here to represent them.
I could go on, Mr. Speaker, but I will respect your observation that I stay on the topic. I will certainly be up to speak on other clauses of the bill as they come before us.

Mr. Speaker, I think we are embarked this evening on a fundamental debate about the rights and privileges of Parliament. In fact, I think those of us on this side of the House who have risen so far have risen basically on questions of privilege. It is my understanding, having been a student of political science for a number of years, that there is a requirement on the government to come to Parliament once a year to raise the revenues it requires. It does this with estimates. It tells us how it is going to spend the money. It is also required, through budgets, to come back every 12 months and to lay out the manner in which it proposes to raise revenues. The measure we have before us tonight is a denial of the general tradition.

Someone used the right word this evening. This measure is repugnant. It is an insult to this House and an insult to every single member in this House that we should be asked to approve this authority now for all time and for the rest of the life of this government. That is what it could very well amount to. If hon. members opposite sneak in this indexing of the tax on beer, wine and tobacco, they will say, "Boy, we outfoxed them on those items; we will get them now on the rest". Indexation of all taxation will then be with us. Inflation will also be with us to stay because it looks very much as if this government had no intention or inclination, and certainly no ability, to deal with inflation. Inflation will be with us as long as this government is here. With inflation and indexation there will be no requirement, when this principle is spread to the rest of the taxation in this country, for this Parliament to assemble. It is that principle we are fighting tonight through this amendment. We are determined that that principle shall not be incorporated in the tax law of this country.
In an earlier intervention I quoted from a letter I received from the Brewers Association of Canada. I use this just as an example. That association is protesting against the proposal to index the excise levies on alcoholic beverages. That is natural, of course, because as inflation continues, there will be increases in levies on beer, and beer is what this association is concerned about. Let me read just a portion of this letter to indicate to the House, to the country, to those in the gallery and to those who read Hansard, just what this will mean in the next decade if this legislation is accepted now, becomes the law of the land and remains unamended for a decade. I refer to this letter dated April 24 from the Brewers Association of Canada. At the bottom of page 3 it says that the minister has also stated he did not believe indexing would affect the stability of the industry. However, one of the effects of the indexing scheme is that it would exacerbate the sales situation existing since the excise levy increased in April of 1980.
In my earlier intervention I indicated that from April of 1980 until January of 1981 there has been a decrease in the sale of beer of 0.36 per cent and an increase in the sale of distilled spirits of 4.6 per cent. I am not so much concerned with that, Mr. Speaker, as I am with this illustration. I come back to the text where it says that by 1991 the price of two dozen small bottles of beer will have increased by 157 per cent.
Let us not forget that indexation is compounded. It is not just a simple application of a percentage on the same base each year, it is the application of that percentage on the incremental base each year. The letter goes on to say that by 1991 the price of two dozen small bottles of beer will have increased by 157 per cent to $23.64, while the price of a 25-ounce bottle of inexpensive gin will have increased by only 100 per cent to $16.42. That is just one instance of what indexation is going to do.
I have in front of me the consumer price index as published in April, 1981, by the bureau of statistics, as we used to call it. The provision we are considering on page 4 of the bill has to do

with the portion of the consumer price index-and I am very much in order, Mr. Speaker-which deals with tobacco and alcohol. I do not quite know what percentage of the index it is, but I will give you the change in the index between April of 1980 and April of 1981 for just that portion. For tobacco and alcohol prices in April of 1980 it was 178.0 on the basis of 1971 equalling 100. In April of 1981, one year later, it was 198.9. Let us say it was 199 for ease of subtraction. Therefore, the difference is 11 per cent.
Now suppose beer and tobacco cost $1. We apply the 11 per cent, and the price becomes $1.11. One year later, inflation has shown no signs of decreasing, so I suspect it would be another 11 per cent. This time the 11 per cent is applied not to $1 but to $1.11; we are compounding.
Now, Mr. Speaker, there is a mystic figure that somebody worked out. I wish I had been the one to do it but I was not. Happily I remember it. The mystic figure in compounding is 72. If you have, say, 11 per cent, you divide that into 72 and you get roughly 6.6. So what happens is that in 6.6 years prices double. That mystic figure of 72 is worth remembering. If the increase were, let us say 15 per cent, divide that into 72 and it is a little less than five. So that in 4.8 years the cost of a commodity would double if the index were increased by 15 per cent a year. Mark you, we are compounding, and this is a very staggering thought.
Now what is the total CPI during that period for all items? In April, 1980, it was 205, and one year later it was 231, a 30 point increase or about 15 per cent over that year. I am making a very rough calculation because we are working with a 200 base here. If this notion is transferred to other tax levies, we are going to see that in four and a half years at 15 per cent, the taxes will be doubled. I hope the people in the gallery realize that and I hope the people watching realize that these are the dangers we are facing tonight. We are facing a completely mute government; not one of the members of the government has risen to comment on any of these matters during the consideration of this amendment-not one of them.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, it will be a simple matter in two or three years for the government to say: "We do not really have to call Parliament because our taxes are rolling in at a pretty good rate". -adjusted or altered in such a manner as the governor in council may, by regulation, prescribe-
Frankly, this clause provides another example of a government ruling by regulation. We have carried this battle in the House since I have been here. Certainly I have been here only a short period of time, but repeatedly the question of the cabinet running the country by regulation and then imposing it without the benefit of the House, because of its Liberal majority, has arisen. This simple clause will provide cabinet with a further power to extend indexed taxation. It is another example of a government ruling by regulation. It is a small item, but it is one that we have opposed vigorously.
When the vote on this clause takes place, I have no doubt that the majority over there will put through this particular provision. Eventually we will wind up with another general statement which allows a great deal of discretionary power and then places that power in the government's hand in the form of regulation. We have dealt with this matter in many bills, whether it was the one my hon. friend brought forward concerning the Bank Act or other legislation. It is not an acceptable procedure in this clause; it is a portrait of arrogance. Literally the government does not know how to compromise or work co-operatively within the parliamentary framework.

We might be dealing strictly with a clause on alcoholic beverages such as beer, wine and spirits, but really what we are talking about, in a rather frank and direct form, is regressive taxation. This is the favourite of the government. Rather than trying to raise funds or revenue in an equitable and fair manner and basically dealing with a progressive taxation system, over the years the government has loaded the burden of taxation on those who can least afford to pay. There is no doubt about the track record of the government. It has displayed a continual moving away from a progressive and fair system of taxation where the raising of government revenue moves out of the corporate sector and into the personal sector. Then in the personal sector it moves down the income scale. Essentially, the rich get richer and the poor face more taxes. Now they are facing an indexed regressive taxation. It is amazing-rule by regulation, continued arrogance, lack of co-operation, and now more and more regressive tax where the burden is loaded on those who can least afford it.
May I call it ten o'clock?
