(A)	PROMOTION OF OFFICERS SERVING AT AIRPORTS
(B)	DIFFERENCE IN TREATMENT OF SENIOR OFFICERS

Mr. Speaker, recently the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Axworthy) introduced a new policy on the basis of a so-called study by which he promoted immigration officers at four international airports from the PM-1 level to the PM-2 level. Those officers now working at Vancouver International Airport, Calgary, Dorval or, of all places, at Mirabel, are automatically working at the PM-2 level without ever having competed for a PM-2 level job.
As a result of a question I asked the minister, I found out that he is still not aware of the whole range of discrimination he has brought about by this change in policy. I questioned the minister in committee about the range of discrimination which he has introduced.
I would like to enumerate a few of the situations which have been brought about by this new policy. New casual employees, that is, those employees who come on staff as summer workers at these airports, immediately begin work at the PM-2 level, while senior officers working at inland ports remain at the PM-1 level just because they happen to be at inland ports. Part-time workers are started at the PM-2 level while fulltime, experienced officers remain at the PM-1 level.
Adjournment Debate
As a result of this policy, it is impossible to make a lateral transfer from an inland port to one of the airports I have mentioned, since transferring from a PM-1 to a PM-2 position would be involved, and the minister told me himself that one would have to compete for that kind of promotion. New recruits who come out of training programs and on to the staff at these airports as full-time employees in the immigration service are immediately senior to the seasoned employees who work at inland ports. The minister says that is all right since one has to compete for these positions. As the minister has said, one must compete for PM-2 positions unless you work at one of these aforementioned airports. Presumably, he is saying that geography is now more important than skill, experience or competition, as long as you are geographically located in the right place and you happen to choose an international airport when you go into the service, rather than an inland port. An officer at an inland port must be a specialist in many kinds of immigration problems, as a PM-1 officer. Meanwhile, the PM-2 officer at one of the airports I have mentioned specializes in only one or two areas, but he becomes a senior officer and automatically receives a higher level of pay.
When it comes to student visas, the PM-2 officer at the airport must only stamp the student's visa, which only takes a few minutes. This is because students who come into the country by way of airplane have had their visas processed by officers in a foreign immigration office who do all the work for the PM-2 officers at the airport. Meanwhile, the PM-1 officer at the inland port must do all the work to introduce a student into the country. He must handle all spontaneous applications for landing a new immigrant, those who come up to the border crossing and say that they have relatives whom they are bringing into the country or that he or she has married an alien and wishes to bring that person into the country. The PM-1 officer must do all the paperwork involved in this type of situation, which is about a four-hour job. The PM-2 officer, the senior officer, even though he is junior to the PM-1 officer at the inland port, gets only a few of these cases, thus avoiding all the paperwork. The skills activity evaluation that the so-called study group did gave this four-hour job four points on the activity scale.
In April, officials rewrote the job descriptions of the officers at Vancouver International Airport, making them counsellors. The same month they wrote a letter saying that these officers will not be doing any counselling because they happened to be PM-2 officers.
In his answer to me as reported in Hansard at page 10012, the minister said that these evaluations "were achieved in very close co-operation with the workers themselves." Mr. Speaker, I suspect the shadows of the evaluators passed by some of these employees, because they never saw them. It is strange that the border passing point at Douglas dropped from number four in activity to number 14 on this new scale of evaluation. How it got ten points below that mausoleum known as Mirabel is beyond me. Douglas, and Pacific Highway processed a total of 258,497 secondary examinations in one year. These officers

are PM-Is. I have three questions to pose to the parliamentary secretary tonight, Mr. Speaker.
First, will a PM-2 be transferred from the Vancouver International Airport to an inland centre as a PM-2?
Second, will or can a PM-1 be transferred to be reclassified to a PM-2 position, and what will happen? Does the officer remain a PM-1?
Third, in order for an inland border PM-1 to transfer into a PM-2 office position, must he compete for a position that was granted to a possibly junior employee and, furthermore, be insulted in the process?

speakeroldname: Mr. Dennis Dawson (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Employment and Immigration):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Employment and Immigration
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the question put by the hon. member, especially since last week, when the Committee on Labour, Manpower and Immigration scrutinized the estimates of the Department of Employment and Immigration, the minister had an opportunity to reply to the hon. member. Understandably, to the hon. member this matter is of tremendous importance, especially since it involves his constituency. But he must also understand that the decision to classify positions at five large Canadian airports, namely Dorval, Mirabel-to which the hon. member referred-Toronto, Calgary and Vancouver, all major ports of entry into Canada, is based on a comparison of examiner workloads involving specific criteria, according to a formula under which are measured the work diversity, complexity and hazards inherent to errors at each point of entry into Canada. As explained by the minister, the formula was developed in total objectivity and with the full co-operation of labour leaders. It is normal in my view that within a department such as ours, studies be undertaken, in co-operation with public servants concerned, in order to determine whether it is possible to arrive at objective criteria to avoid discrimination between the major and problem ports of entry across Canada.
Clearly, when Mirabel is compared to certain border points of entry into Canada, it is realized that conditions there are much more complex. There is no question there of immigrants or visitors from the United States, but complex cases from abroad. The Treasury Board has approved the formula, which meets current criteria in the classification standards for groups PM, PM-1, PM-2 and PM-3, as well as classification principles in force in the Public Service. A review of conditions in all points of entry will be made in April 1982, two years after the implementation of the new formula. Certainly, the Department will consider representations such as those made by the hon. member. The situation is very well understood, and everything will be done to ensure that there is no discrimination against people, whether from his constituency, from an airport, or from a port of entry into Canada where problems may be somewhat easier to solve.

NATIONAL CAPITAL-DELAY RESPECTING RIDEAU CENTRE DEVELOPMENT PROJECT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on March 5, I directed a question to the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Cosgrove) concerning the long awaited and much needed Rideau Centre development in my riding. My question had been prompted by press reports to the effect that the Rideau Centre development had been put off once more because of legal and administrative problems. The Rideau Centre has been the subject of several interventions in the House by myself of course, as this is my riding. I must say that this development has received the almost unanimous support of hon. members from both sides of the House, Liberal as well as Progressive Conservative, in the national capital area, at least on the Ontario side.
Hon. members have often heard me deal with this subject over the past eight or nine years. The least people can say about the Rideau Centre is that it remains an audacious, original and extremely complex project which seeks to revive an important part of the very core of our national capital. The idea to develop federal lands, in co-operation with the private sector, has progressed considerably over the past eight or nine years. The Rideau Centre project was introduced at the initiative of the National Capital Commission and approved by cabinet in July 1973. Therefore, it is nothing new. Over the years, all levels of government have been consulted and involved, and have co-operated with citizens' groups and representatives of the industry in the study and preparation of the general plans for the development of the Rideau Centre. There was no lack of publicity about the project, especially when they had to cope with difficult problems and it appeared to be in danger. Indeed that is what prompted me to ask the minister the question on March 5, because certain media were saying that the project was again in the throes of death. The problems have been numerous. All groups at all levels had to be conciliatory. There were intensive consultations on the ways and means to carry out this very important project the purpose of which is to revitalize a very fashionable neighbourhood of Ottawa which is in my riding of Ottawa-Vanier.
In fact, the aim of all those who support the Rideau Centre project is to reverse the North American trend of letting city cores decay or even die. Everyone involved in this project has worked toward a general design, making the downtown area stimulating and prosperous. For this to happen, it must be a people's place, a place people can call home, living and working here in peace and security. The city core as an attractive and vibrant spot should be a magnet for visitors.
Statistics published in 1971 convinced the federal government it had a duty to help transform downtown Ottawa. In 1961, the central business area of Ottawa accounted for 65 per cent of total department stores sales in the national capital
June 4, 1981

region. Ten years later, this figure had shrunk to 31 per cent, and by 1976 the latest statistics we have, the figure was 22 per cent. This decline in spite of increasing revenues, salaries and population in the region demonstrated to us, at least, that downtown Ottawa was dying.
During times of economic difficulties as we are experiencing at present, it is not easy to mount a scheme costing hundreds of millions of dollars and create several thousands jobs. The Rideau Centre itself will create 2,000 or 3,000 jobs on site and off the site. It will stimulate the economy of Ottawa and the region. As well, it will provide an attractive, stable and yet lively milieu.
In a way, the Rideau Centre began with the renovation of the historical section, Sussex Drive and the Byward market. In this zone, new shops and apartments are already occupied. Restored old buildings have been put to modern use, several restaurants and boutiques are prospering, and I am convinced that the Rideau Centre will bring new economic and social life to the district. The Rideau Centre project offers possibilities for employment diversification. For example, it will create further employment opportunities in the tourist industry. The construction of a congress centre will attract various groups and associations throughout North America and hopefully Europe, for meetings and conventions here in Ottawa. Tourism provides spin-offs in many areas, other than those directly related to hotels, restaurants and transportation. Retail and wholesale trade and other commercial and business services benefit from tourism.
I anticipate something constructive happening with this project. I want to thank all members who have assisted and supported this project, but special mention must be made of the hon. member for Nepean-Carleton (Mr. Baker) for his constant support. I think he joins with many of us in hoping that this project will come to a successful conclusion and that it will alleviate the economic and other difficulties we have in the national capital at this time.
[ Translation]
Mr. Speaker, I think I ought to point out that, from an economic standpoint, the construction of the Rideau Centre will create several thousand permanent jobs. The Centre will bring in several million dollars annually in taxes and property taxes at all levels of government. It is a challenging project, but not easy to carry out. I know that the Minister of Public Works and all his colleagues who held that portfolio before him have worked very hard to see this project through. I also know that for over a year now legal complexities have often jeopardized the success of this project and I was told that the minister has worked unremittingly in attempting to find a satisfactory solution. Therefore I would like to hear the minister bring us up to date on the situation of the project and perhaps pass along encouraging and interesting news.
Adjournment Debate

speakeroldname: Hon. Paul J. Cosgrove (Minister of Public Works):
speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
subtopic: NATIONAL CAPITAL-DELAY RESPECTING RIDEAU CENTRE DEVELOPMENT PROJECT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it gives me great pleasure to reply to the hon. member for Ottawa-Vanier (Mr. Gauthier) that after seven years of hard planning and negotiations, the signing of the documents will take place tomorrow, thus permitting the Rideau Centre project to proceed.
As the hon. member for Ottawa-Vanier has said, the centre is a large real estate complex to be developed largely on Crown lands. This 14-acre site within view of Parliament will become the nucleus of a much larger plan involving major improvements to municipal infrastructure services, vehicular, public transit and pedestrian systems, not to mention several private sector commercial developments in the Rideau area. In this instance the Crown has sold its lands to the private sector and has retained certain air rights over the project. The Crown has the right to repurchase its lands with all of the buildings for $1 in 52 years.
Our objective was to revitalize the eastern core of the nation's capital, to create permanent employment and to work for the construction industry in addition to promoting the use of idle federal lands. In addition to the hotel complex described by the member and in addition to the 650,000 square feet of retail space, which includes the Eaton department store and the Congress Centre, there will be 1,500 parking spaces, a transit mall and pedestrian walkways.
The project will create approximately 2,000 person-years of construction work on the federal lands between 1981 and 1983 and another 1,000 person-years work for the construction industry in general for this region as a spin-off in the support industry. This project will create permanent employment for approximately 1,500 people.
The federal participation is $19 million from public works and $11 milion from the National Capital Commission. The private sector and other levels of government will contribute over $173 million to the project.
I would like to acknowledge the very significant role of the chairman of the National Capital Commission, the Hon. Bud Drury, former minister of public works, in the project and the support of the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin) and the hon. member who has asked the question. As well, credit is due my officials in the Public Works and other ministries who have demonstrated resourcefulness in bringing this project to fruition.
In summary, the Rideau Centre will be an attraction and a boon, not only for the residents of the national capital region but for all residents of Canada and abroad who visit our national capital. Most important, construction begins on Monday.

Adjournment Debate EMPLOYMENT
(A) TRAINING AGREEMENTS WITH INDUSTRIAL ASSOCIATIONS (B) NEED FOR CO-OPERATION WITH LABOUR UNIONS

subtopic: NATIONAL CAPITAL-DELAY RESPECTING RIDEAU CENTRE DEVELOPMENT PROJECT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in the early part of May, the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Axworthy) announced agreement with the coal mining, shipbuilding and aerospace industries for co-operative programs to train skilled workers in order to meet the shortages in those industries. The press briefings which were provided with the announcement said that these are "endeavours by industry, labour and government" to meet the needs of the industry for skilled workers. My question arises from the fact that I was unable to find, when the announcements were made, that there had in fact been any consultation or discussion with the unions representing the workers concerned. All of these industries are industries in which virtually all the production employees are organized and belong to unions. The government has repeatedly indicated it wants the co-operation of business and labour.
We have had intensive studies by joint government, industry and labour committees of a series of individual important industries in Canada. We have had a major study done by labour and management committees into the needs to meet the financial and human needs for the megaprojects we expect to see in the next two generations.
Yet when it comes down to the actual planning, the department by design or by omission completely ignored the unions which represent the workers now in the industry.
Let me quote for a moment a couple of clauses from the agreement with the coal association. I quote as follows from the general agreement:
That employment and career opportunities created will be made available, firstly, to employees of the respective member companies in which the opportunities are created, and secondly, to Canadian citizens or other permanent residents;
If you are going to make opportunities available for skills or upgrading of employees now working in the companies which are organized by unions, this cannot be done without consultation with the unions which represent the workers. I say that not to have brought the unions in right from the beginning was an error of major proportions.
There is a clause which states:
That Affirmative Action/Special Measures will actively be promoted among participating member companies, whenever possible.
Again, that certainly cannot work in a friendly co-operative spirit without the co-operation of the unions. That was not done and to my knowledge it has not been done until now.
I asked the minister a second question having to do with an earlier announcement last January that there would be a $350 million industrial training program for hard-hit areas which included Windsor, Sept-Isles and Sydney, Nova Scotia. Again, when that program was announced, in checking with unions I found they had not been consulted. That was last January. When I raised the question on May 20 I was told by the minister that whatever had happened in the past, the community committee in Windsor where the auto workers are so vitally involved was working.
Just in the last day or so I spoke with the representative of the auto workers' union in Windsor, and I can tell the parliamentary secretary to the minister that he is completely dissatisfied with the role which the union is being permitted to fill. Today I received a report from a senior member of the steelworkers' union of the national office in connection with the two other cities involved in that industrial adjustment program. He reported that in Sept-Isles there was some talk about a committee being set up and a chairman appointed, that there might be involvement with the union but that so far there has been no action. In Sydney, he says, there is no news. Some initial announcement was made, but there was no real follow-up, and the little information they received was considered "a bunch of junk".
I say that this program is doomed to failure unless the government is seriously committed to doing what it has always said, and that is to encourage and to require the full co-operation of unions, not after the plans are made and not after the contracts are signed, sealed and delivered, but right from the beginning when the idea is conceived and when the government department begins to consult with the industry. Just at the same time the government must begin to consult with the union. Otherwise the programs are doomed to failure.

Mr. Speaker, I hope you understand that we are in complete disagreement with the hon. member because, as Your Honour knows, and as has been stated in the House by the minister, officials of the labour organizations were immediately contacted concerning-I will start with the second case-the cases to which the hon. member referred regarding Sydney, Sept-Iles and Windsor. The officials were contacted right after the March 16 announcement designating Port-Cartier-Sept-Iles, Tracey-Sorel, Sydney and Windsor for special adjustment assistance.
More specifically, for the community of Port-Cartier-Sept-iles-

With respect to Port-Cartier and Sept-Iles, Mr. Speaker, I can assure you that the Canadian Paperworkers International Union, local 1125, the Federation des travailleurs du Quebec, local 8399 and the United Steelworkers of America were all consulted on their involvement in the community adjustment aid committee for Port-Cartier and Sept-Iles.

In Sydney, Nova Scotia, the Cape Breton Labour Council and the United Steelworkers of America were contacted concerning their participation on a community adjustment committee for that community. The Confederation des Syndicats Nationaux, La Federation de Travailleurs de Quebec and United Steelworkers of America were contacted in relation to their participation in the projects for Tracey-Sorel.

In Windsor, consultations were with the Windsor and District Labour Council, the Canadian Council of United Auto Workers and the Essex and Kent County Building and Construction Trades Council, which are members of the community adjustment committee for that community.

Mr. Speaker, the minister said to this House on May 20, 1981, in answer to a question from the hon. member for Winnipeg-North (Mr. Orlikow) that the conclusion of agreements with the aeronautical industry and the coal mining and other mining companies regarding manpower planning is one of the most important initiatives ever taken by this government for efficient human resources planning in order to fullfil the need for skilled manpower in some industrial sectors.
Both management and labour unions, contrary to what the hon. member said, actively participated in the negotiation process through the two members of the Employment and Immigration Commission, one acting on behalf of the unions, the other on behalf of industry.
Adjournment Debate
I should like to point out, however, that manpower planning is usually the responsibility of management, and that those agreements are intended solely to serve as a general framework within which government and industry can co-operate. The provisions for training are meant to give the companies involved information on the training programs offered by the commission. Specific manpower planning and training programs will be implemented by each company and in every case, as in the past, Mr. Speaker, both unions and employers will be consulted. I believe this refutes easily the allegations of the hon. member. I am sure those programs will be implemented without delay: we can then find out whether or not the communities involved were consulted.
